Armenia to feel impact of Russian export restrictions in 2H 2026 — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:14:36 UTC
14:14:36 KST

MOSCOW, August 18. /TASS/. The impact of restrictions on exports of Armenia’s products to Russia will become apparent for on Armenia in statistics for the second half of 2026, associate professor at the HSE University Faculty of Economic Sciences Anna Fedyunina told TASS.
"Clearly, the pronounced effect on Armenian exports to Russia will emerge specifically in the second half of 2026, when the restrictions take effect and affect a significant share of seasonal shipments of berries, vegetables and fruit," the expert said.
The restrictions were introduced in stages from late May and throughout June 2026. "They gradually covered tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, herbs and strawberries, followed by stone fruits and grapes, as well as potatoes, dried fruit, certain types of fish products, alcoholic beverages and mineral water," Fedyunina recalled. At the same time, in the first five months of 2026, exports to Russia of goods in categories that were subsequently subject to restrictions increased compared with the same period of 2025.
According to Fedyunina, this trend may be linked to the effect of anticipatory shipments.
According to calculations by the HSE University Center for Structural Policy Research based on UN Comtrade data at FOB prices, Armenian exports totaled $2.86 bln in January-May 2026, down 3.7% from the same period of 2025. "At the same time, the decline accelerated to 11.6% year-on-year in May. Thus, for now, this is more a matter of exports stabilizing after the sharp contraction of 2025 than a new precipitous decline," the expert noted.
Data for the first five months of 2026 also show no sharp decline in Armenian exports to Russia so far. "According to our estimates, Armenian exports to Russia totaled $1.1776 bln in the first five months of 2024, $1.0783 bln in the same period of 2025 and $1.0288 bln in 2026. Thus, compared with 2025, the decline amounted to about 4.6%, while compared with 2024, it was about 12.6%," she concluded.

The Geran Seeker series represents the continued development of technologies based on the platform, with the Geran serving as a universal carrier. China moves to unlock county-level consumption, energize domestic demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
13:03:47 CST
14:03:47 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 18 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday unveiled a set of measures to unlock the consumption potential of counties and smaller cities, tapping the vast lower-tier markets as a new source of domestic demand and economic growth.
The government calls for upgrading consumption channels in counties, including renovating township commercial centers, rural markets and local fairs, encourages domestic and international brands to open regional debut stores, and promotes the redevelopment of existing land resources to improve services, according to a guideline jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce and other authorities.
The guideline also urges better services that cater to the elderly and children, more efficient urban-rural distribution networks, and stronger county-level employment, as well as more channels for residents to increase their incomes.
The measures come as China seeks to give consumption a bigger role in driving economic growth.
The lower-tier markets, generally referring to third-tier and smaller cities, counties, townships and rural areas, account for about 70 percent of China's population and 60 percent of total retail sales of consumer goods. These markets have emerged as a key link between urban and rural economies and an important part of the domestic economic cycle.
The lower-tier markets have diverse needs across different levels, said Shen Bing, a researcher at an institute under the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), noting that this diversity can provide broad room for businesses to develop new service models while creating new momentum for consumption.
Official data showed that retail sales of consumer goods in rural areas rose 2.4 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, 1.3 percentage points faster than in urban areas. County-and township-level retail sales were estimated to account for nearly 40 percent of the country's total.
China's 2,800-plus county-level administrative divisions form a vast and diverse domestic market, said Chen Xi, a researcher with the NDRC, noting that consumption upgrade is gradually extending from major cities to county-level markets, providing an endogenous source of consumption growth. ■

Pocket-sized sensors and mobile apps are changing how Londoners track air pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:02:52 UTC
14:02:52 KST

Portable pollution sensors are opening up places once impossible to monitor, from Tube platforms to school playgrounds.
In most countries, air pollution is still one of the biggest threats to people's health. In London, things have been getting better - and that's largely down to tougher transport rules.
An independent analysis by experts from Imperial College London found that the Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ), which keeps the most polluting vehicles off the road, has cut levels of fine particle pollution (PM 2.5) by 31 per cent in outer London and nitrogen dioxide, the traffic-linked gas that irritates the lungs, by 27 per cent across the city.
But air quality can change throughout the day, and that goes for ozone, pollen and other pollutants too.
Air quality sensors reach new places
Keeping up with these swings is getting easier, thanks to a new generation of air quality sensors - compact, and comparatively affordable, though still priced in the tens of thousands of euros.
Dr Kayla Schulte is a Social and Environmental Technology researcher at Imperial College London. Her fieldwork relies on devices like a handheld black carbon monitor, a compact sensor that logs particle pollution from burning materials like wood or coal.
"We have lower levels of black carbon here in the UK," she tells Euronews Earth. "It is definitely more of an issue globally and contributes to very high numbers of deaths."
These small sensors - now used across the UK capital's 'Breathe London' monitoring network - can go where bulky reference equipment never could.
"Having small compact equipment like these sensors really changes where and how we're able to monitor pollution," Schulte says, pointing to colleagues who now measure air quality inside the London Underground.
Their size also makes it easier to put sensors right where they're needed most: in the communities carrying the heaviest pollution burden. And software developers can plug the readings into their own apps and platforms, making air quality something people can actually check on their phone, wherever they are in London.
Making pollution data clearer and more accessible
For Schulte, that's an important point - it matters that the public actually sees the data the sensors produce. "Certain groups in society are more likely to interact with information about pollution when they're caring for an individual that might have a health issue," she says. But plenty of people who could benefit from real-time data simply never come across it.
Part of the problem, she argues, is how that data gets published: "The way that air pollution information is presented can be very, very complex."
Her team works directly with affected communities to fix that, running school activities where pupils design their own pollution displays, and collaborating with residents on the AWAIR project - a set of solar-powered public air quality displays now installed across several London neighbourhoods.
More rollouts are planned, as researchers try to close the gap between what sensors can measure and what the public can actually understand.

Nômade Temple Ibiza wants to return to the island’s “deeper history” which is “rooted in freedom, creativity and connection”.

Located in Portinatx in the Spanish island’s north, the 182-key property has direct access to a secluded beach.
The design of the new hotel preserves iconic elements of the original resort found here, such as arches and terraces, and the project as a whole is meant to “look back to a time when the island functioned as a meeting point for creative communities, where music, art and human connection shaped everyday life”.
Blending wellness, music and gastronomy, Nômade Temple Ibiza will offer retreats, artist residences and ritual events throughout the year.
“We are not interested in replicating the predictable luxury model that defines much of Ibiza today,” Miguel Isla, CEO of Nomade People, said.
“The island has a deeper history – one rooted in freedom, creativity and connection – and that’s what we want to bring back.”
The brand already has hotels in Tulum and Holbox in Mexico, as well as a property in Madrid.
What to expect at Nômade Temple Ibiza
In a bid to minimise its ecological footprint, the culinary team at Nômade Temple Ibiza works with local fishermen, producers and growers across its restaurants.
This includes omakase KUU JŪ, which makes use of Mediterranean ingredients such as red prawns, citrus and island herbs across its Japanese-style plates, as well as all-day dining spot TAVLA, which focuses on charcoal-grilled meats, marinated seafood and seasonal vegetables.
If you’re looking to take advantage of Ibiza’s fantastic weather, you can head to 4FU3GOS, a beachside restaurant with a seafood-heavy menu, while one of the property’s highlights is Dante’s Hifi, which has been inspired by Japanese listening bars.
Café Libre is where you’ll start your day, with healthy breakfast dishes, specialty coffee and smoothies.
The resort is also home to GÖN House of Healing Ibiza, the wellness area that includes hammam steam rooms, dry saunas, cold plunges and a warm mineral water flotation tank, as well as treatment rooms for facials and massages.
Nômade Temple Ibiza is a 40-minute drive from Ibiza Airport. The international airport is served year-round from domestic destinations including Madrid, Barcelona, Malaga and Valencia, with seasonal connections from major cities including Athens, Rome, Frankfurt, London, Milan and more.
The opening certainly isn’t the only new property welcoming guests to Ibiza this year. Other must-book stays include the Parador de Ibiza, which is found within the city’s UNESCO World Heritage-listed acropolis, and the five-star BLESS Ibiza The Site in Playa d’en Bossa.

====================================================================================================

Sydney music venues closing rapidly as owners seek 'DIY' alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:01:49 UTC
14:01:49 KST

Sydney small venue owners seek DIY alternatives to closing down
The live music community in Sydney has been devastated over the past 12 months.
At least eight venues have closed their doors, drastically reducing the number of smaller-capacity rooms in the city.
They are places where bands and artists cut their teeth, try out new music, and potentially get scouted for larger rooms.
They are also where fans discover new artists and support their local scene.
Sydney's music ecosystem struggled as spaces like Mary's Underground, People's Republic, Lazy Thinking and MoshPit turned the lights off for various reasons, including skyrocketing insurance and rental costs, evictions and noise restrictions.
Many of the venues were beholden to a landlord, and the risks that came with operating in a rented space.
Despite government grants, council support, fundraising and more, smaller-capacity venues are barely breaking even, let alone turning a profit.
Eventually, something has got to give.
How bad is it in Sydney?
SydneyMusic co-founder Joe Hardy has seen the closures across the city through the not-for-profit's extensive gig guide, showing that shuttered venues held more than 690 live music events between July 2025 and June 2026.
"They're all different problems between them," Hardy said.
"It's very easy to just look at them and go, 'That's just all the same thing,' but no. When you actually dive into it, they've all had different root causes.
"Some of them have been really successful from audience and engagement perspectives, but then you have landlord issues and then others do have real problems with an aging-out demographic."
Among the recent closures was Lazy Thinking; a bar, venue and record store that focused on providing a space for independent Australian artists.
The venue rarely broke even and lost money every month it was open over the past three years, which didn't deter venue owner Jim Flanagan.
He made it work with a "handful of extraordinary donors, the occasional government grant, one-off donations and, increasingly, our members".
In July, the space was featured in a Guardian article about music lovers having to "adapt or die" in the face of a changing environment.
One month later, Flanagan announced the closure of Lazy Thinking after receiving an eviction notice from the venue's landlords.
Told to vacate by the end of the year, Flanagan instead decided to shut up shop at the end of August and spend the rest of the year taking stock and working towards how the space could exist again in a new, more permanent and sustainable venue.
"Part of me was like, 'You know what, what's the point of continuing? I need to fundraise like a crazy person every month to keep the venue afloat and Lazy Thinking more generally,'" Flanagan said.
"I don't think it's a useful use of my or other people involved in Lazy Thinking's energy to … do all this work to subsidise a space that we know we're going to lose.
"I do not think the economics of running a small music venue in Sydney right now works at all.
"I wish I was wrong, [but] we are seeing that every day with more venues."
A city-wide situation
It's not just spaces that host emerging acts that are feeling the ever-growing pressure of trying to exist in Sydney's stressful economic climate.
Earlier this year, Mary's Underground, which has provided a stage to artists like Gordi, High Vis, Bad//Dreems and more, announced it would be closing after seven years in Sydney's CBD.
Alongside Mary's Underground, the team also books Liberty Hall, a 1,200-capacity venue opposite Hordern Pavilion.
"It's concerning in terms of like, where's the bridging venues for developing Australian artists to get to that level of room?" said Tom Gordon, director of music and programming.
"Also, playing a stage of that level and then jumping up to a Liberty Hall or something along those lines is a pretty wild jump to take."
With the closure of smaller rooms reducing the pool of spaces where emerging bands can get a gig, other venues will likely have to be more selective when booking shows.
Gordon said venue spaces of similar size to the 500-capacity Oxford Art Factory would survive.
"[When spaces] like Mary's Underground disappear, inadvertently shows will go there, which is great," he said.
"We're happy about that. But then Oxford Art Factory is going to be booked every single day of the week, and they're going to prioritise the shows that sell the most tickets.
"So, a lot of those local communities are going to have to move towards DIY [Do It Yourself] because there isn't another option."
DIY common thread
Sydney's music scenes seem to be turning to the do-it-yourself approach at a community level in the face of traditional venues closing.
Musicians, independent record labels and fans are being creative in finding spaces for live music, drawing on decades of experience from historic DIY scenes that have propped up punk, hardcore and electronic music in Australia.
From gigs in backyards and lounge rooms to acoustic shows in parks, skate bowls and empty warehouses, people are finding ways to plug in, play music and build community.
"You don't have scenes building in the same way inside traditional venue architecture," Hardy said.
"I think the thing that's really proving this point is what's happening in the DIY space, which I think in the last 24 months has really seen a resurgence to a degree.
"It's hard to plot even for me because it's all happening in real time and you sort of see a lot of the effects in retrospect."
"I would like to see DIY stop being demonised. In fact, I would like to see it being actively encouraged and fostered."
Entertainment precinct approach
While high rents and insurance are deeper systemic issues, the Inner West Council has been working to ease pressures controlled at its level.
Special entertainment precincts (SEPs) have been trialled along the Enmore Road strip over the past three years, and have expanded to other areas including Balmain, Marrickville and Dulwich Hill to help boost creative communities.
The precincts allow venues to run under extended trading hours, council-regulated sound allowances, and within specified zones that offer extra protection from noise complaints and other external risks that come with operating a venue.
Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne is working with the City of Sydney to mark Newtown's King Street as a special entertainment precinct.
He said other councils across NSW were planning their own SEPs, including Byron Bay, Randwick and Burwood, which he said was an "interesting case".
"Burwood Road is extraordinarily lively late at night," he said.
"It's going well, but it's a different culture. It's very ethnically diverse and the night-time activity is far less dependent on alcohol.
"That's change that we're seeing across the board with younger people having a healthier relationship with alcohol than previous generations.
"But that doesn't mean they don't want to go out late at night and it doesn't mean that they are not interested in live music.
"So governments, including local councils, need to think carefully about what are we going to do to cultivate spaces and venues for younger people who do want to be out in the public domain and on the streets late at night, but they don't necessarily want to do it through getting pissed at the pub."
Looking abroad for answers
Internationally, music communities have formed initiatives like the Music Venue Trust, a UK charity that aims to protect and nurture local live music through the purchasing of long-term venues, ensuring their existence.
While an initiative like this is something that is yet to exist in Australia, Cr Byrne has encouraged councils across the country to follow the Inner West Council and allow town halls and other council-run spaces to be used for creative purposes.
"We've had thousands of artists making use of those facilities, which has been good," he said.
"[They are] public institutions that have huge heritage value and we have to invest very large sums in maintaining and upgrading, but they were sitting dormant 80 or 90 per cent of the time.
"Opening them up for artistic use has been a good thing, something I would encourage councils across New South Wales to do. Every council has a town hall. Some of them have multiple town halls, and mostly they're sitting unused for large slabs of time."

====================================================================================================

Want to retire in your 40s? Young workers are turning to FIRE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

As more employees face workplace burnout or choose to pursue passion projects, FIRE is increasingly becoming a way to achieve financial independence early.
Rising inflation, higher interest rates and the cost-of-living squeeze felt across much of the world have pushed more young people to explore alternative paths to financial independence, escaping the rat race to focus on what they're passionate about.
Growing geopolitical instability in recent years, including the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, has also underlined the need for a solid financial cushion and multiple back-up options in case of the unexpected.
Together, these pressures have fuelled the rise of the Financial Independence, Retire Early (FIRE) movement, increasingly adopted by younger people looking to plan ahead and reach their financial goals sooner.
Why are more people choosing FIRE?
In many parts of the world, higher housing costs and stagnant wages have made traditional retirement feel out of reach for entire generations.
According to a recent YouGov survey, 57% to 72% of non-retired non-retired adults across Europe lack confidence that they will ever be able to live comfortably in retirement.
This has led more people to take direct control of their finances, reducing the risk of old-age poverty.
Many also face serious workplace burnout, driven by corporate stress, long commutes and a lack of proper work-life balance.
Younger workers increasingly value free time, travel, personal projects and meaningful work over endlessly climbing the corporate ladder or accumulating status symbols.
Better tools, such as low-fee index funds and online finance communities, have also made financial education, tracking and wealth-building far easier than for earlier generations, despite added geopolitical volatility.
Who is FIRE for?
FIRE suits certain kinds of people. One group is high earners with low expenses, including professionals in tech, engineering, medicine or finance who can bank a high salary while keeping their lifestyle modest.
Another is the natural optimisers: people who enjoy tracking numbers, planning for the long term and budgeting, and who already have some grounding in personal finance.
Employees already facing intense workplace stress who see financial freedom as an exit strategy could also benefit from adopting FIRE, where possible. Similarly, people looking to pursue creative projects, travel or volunteer work without worrying about a regular income could benefit too.
How can you follow FIRE principles?
The FIRE movement relies on two main methods — the 25x rule and the 4% rule — to calculate how much you need to retire comfortably, and how much you can safely withdraw each year during retirement.
The 25x rule involves multiplying your estimated annual living expenses by 25. The resulting total is your FIRE number: the investment portfolio size you need to stop working.
The 4% rule, meanwhile, says to withdraw 4% of your total portfolio in your first year of early retirement. That amount should then be adjusted for inflation every subsequent year, which helps prevent your savings running out over a standard retirement timeline.
In general, FIRE aspirers adopt extreme saving habits, often putting aside 50% to 70% of their net income during their working years. They are also highly frugal, ruthlessly cutting unnecessary spending to lower their baseline annual expenses — which in turn lowers their overall FIRE target.
Many also invest aggressively, choosing low-cost stock indexes and tax-advantaged accounts to make the most of compound growth.
Broadly, there are four types of FIRE strategy.
The first, Lean FIRE, is for minimalists and budget-conscious individuals who want to live on very little — under €30,000 a year, for example — in order to retire as fast as possible.
There is also Fat FIRE, for high earners who refuse to compromise on comfort. These people usually aim for a much larger nest egg to maintain a luxurious or high-spend lifestyle.
Barista FIRE is for people who want to quit corporate life but keep working in some capacity, taking on part-time roles for extra cash or benefits such as health insurance.
Coast FIRE suits younger workers who want to stop actively saving early: they invest heavily upfront and let compound interest carry them the rest of the way to a traditional retirement age.
What to keep in mind before adopting FIRE
While financial independence and early retirement may sound attractive, there are several things to consider before adopting FIRE.
Because the movement can require saving up to 70% of your income and living on a strict budget, people who adopt FIRE need to be highly disciplined, and prepared to plan for decades of healthcare costs and inflation without a traditional paycheque.
Frugality and extreme saving, especially at a young age, can also raise the risk of social isolation, which can be difficult to manage.
Market fluctuations and crashes can change expected returns too, particularly in the early years of saving and investing.
Some people may also face identity loss, especially if they have recently left the labour market and find themselves without a clear daily purpose.
And despite the best-laid plans, some FIRE adherents find they need to re-enter the workforce after years or decades away — which can be difficult if skills, knowledge and professional networks have gone stale.

As Europe’s rivers hit record lows, what does the future hold for Lithuania’s waterways?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

While this summer's headlines have focused on record-low water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Vistula, Lithuania's own rivers have been in slow decline for three decades – a trend scientists say will accelerate as the climate warms further, regardless of how much rain falls in any given year.
A record-breaking summer
Europe is warming faster than any other continent on Earth, and this summer has driven the point home. The EU's Copernicus climate monitoring service reported on August 10 that June and July were the hottest ever recorded in western Europe, with average temperatures across the two months reaching 21.62C, beating the previous record set in 2022.
Climatologist Professor Arūnas Bukantis says the shrinking of major western and central European rivers is no longer an unusual event – it's becoming a regular one.
"These extreme low-water episodes have been happening for perhaps three decades now, and they crop up in one river after another – French rivers, the Rhine, the Vistula, the Danube. These events are now very frequent, and naturally that disrupts shipping. In general, when river flow drops, water for irrigation and for cooling power stations starts to run short too," he said.
He attributes the trend to climate change bringing more frequent heatwaves and droughts to Europe, compounded by low rainfall and heightened evaporation during prolonged hot spells.
A three-decade decline, driven by evaporation
Gediminas Sližys, head of hydrological observations at the Lithuanian Hydrometeorological Service, says the country isn't currently experiencing a hydrological drought.
But on one stretch of the Nemunas – Lithuania's longest river, which flows south to north through the country before reaching the Baltic Sea near Kaunas and Klaipėda – near the southern town of Druskininkai, water levels are running 40cm below the mid-August average.
"That's reached the point where the water level is now damaging to nature, damaging to the whole ecosystem," Sližys said, adding that scientists are still investigating the cause.
One theory: water being held back at a hydroelectric plant across the border in Belarus, near Grodno. A stretch of the Nemunas near Smalininkai, close to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, has also reached similarly low levels.
Despite adequate average rainfall this summer, Sližys and Bukantis both point to a slow, three-decade decline in Lithuania's river levels – driven, they say, not by falling rainfall but by rising evaporation.
"Rainfall seems to fall in the amounts needed, or sometimes even more than usual, but the flow keeps decreasing and river levels drop by tens of centimetres in summer, because water evaporates from the soil before it can reach the groundwater. So the underground feed into our rivers is now weaker," Bukantis said.
"This has been a consistent downward trend since the late 20th century, even though rainfall itself hasn't fallen."
Droughts, Sližys adds, have always occurred in Lithuania, but they're now longer and more frequent.
"September now behaves hydrologically like an extension of summer – river levels in September look just like they do in summer."
He also points to milder winters: prolonged snow cover used to replenish water reserves each spring, but that effect has weakened, with last winter a rare exception to the trend.
What comes next
Asked what Lithuania's rivers might look like in 20 years, both scientists point to more of the same: longer, more frequent droughts and continued falls in water levels.
"These effects will only intensify. Heatwaves will be more frequent, more intense, longer-lasting. And rivers certainly won't gain water – only lose it. Lakes often shrink in summer too," Bukantis said.
Sližys expects more small rivers to dry up completely each summer – a phenomenon already seen on smaller waterways in northern and central Lithuania, including the Yslykis, Dotnuvėlė and Nova.
"Looking ahead, given the climate trends under way, these events will recur, and the list of smaller rivers drying up completely in summer will grow," he said.
A headache for river shipping
Commercial freight shipping is only lightly developed on Lithuania's rivers, so falling water levels rarely make headlines the way they do on the Rhine. But Bukantis recalls years when prolonged drought made river navigation impossible even for small tourist boats: "There have been times when the navigable channel – I mean on the Nemunas, the Neris – was left with depths of just a metre, a metre and a half."
Sližys identifies the riskiest stretches as the Nemunas near Birštonas and Druskininkai, and the Neris – which flows through the capital, Vilnius – near the city centre.
Vilnius wants to dredge the river running through its capital
Consequently, Vilnius city council is pressing ahead with plans to dredge a stretch of the Neris running through the capital, between Vingis Park and Valakampiai II beach.
Mayor Valdas Benkunskas told LRT.lt earlier this year that the river's potential is under-used, and that dredging would make it easier to open the waterway to boat traffic and turn it into more of a draw for tourists and locals alike.
The council says it has identified specific spots along the waterway that are difficult to navigate, and plans to clear sediment to make passage safer.
"It's worth stressing that the planned works are minimal and safety-focused. The plan is only to remove built-up sediment and hazardous objects – for example, large items such as concrete blocks of unclear origin that have been found in some spots, and which pose a real risk to navigation," the council said in a statement to LRT.lt.
An environmental impact assessment for the project, commissioned from Lithuania's Environmental Protection Agency, is still under way, with no final conclusions yet.
Asked whether climate scientists had been, or would be, consulted on the long-term effects of climate change on the Neris – given three decades of falling water levels across Lithuania's rivers, including the Neris itself, and forecasts pointing to more of the same – the council did not respond directly, though it said researchers, environmental experts and relevant authorities would be involved in the assessment process, alongside public consultations.
Scientists: dredging is, at best, a temporary fix
Given that climate change is intensifying and Lithuania's rivers are gradually shrinking, with conditions worsening further in summer in some spots, Bukantis argues that developing shipping on the country's largest rivers would be a risky bet.
Sližys agrees that dredging the Neris would only ever be a stop-gap. "This would only help temporarily, at a particular point in time – but fundamentally, water levels tend to run lower than usual in summer anyway. So carrying out this kind of technical intervention doesn't really gain us much," he said.
Bukantis goes further, warning the project could do serious environmental harm.
"This project really shouldn't even be under consideration, let alone carried out, because there's a real risk of disrupting the entire hydrographic and ecological system of the Neris once dredging work like this begins. People shouldn't imagine the Neris could become some kind of shipping artery – it's simply too small a river for that, and its natural course should be left alone. Drastic engineering interventions like this can disrupt how the river functions, and pose a particular threat to spawning grounds and fish populations," he said.
He adds that any dredging would likely be short-lived regardless, since the cleared stretch would simply silt up again – during spring floods, for instance – rendering the work largely pointless while still damaging the riverbank system through new embankments that distort the river's course.
"It stops being a natural river and becomes an excavated channel instead... It's essentially a project that absorbs public money while being environmentally damaging and economically pointless," Bukantis said.
What could actually help?
Setting the dredging project aside, what could genuinely help Lithuania's rivers and other water bodies adapt to a changing climate?
Sližys points to hydroelectric power plants, whose management directly affects downstream water levels – better regulation of them, he argues, could partly offset the impact of droughts on the country's waterways.
"At the moment, our system makes it difficult to hold hydroelectric plant operators to account, when what they should be doing during droughts is releasing water downstream rather than generating electricity – and not holding water back, because every time they do, it drains the river further."
He notes that this is complicated by the fact that some of Lithuania's rivers, including the Nemunas, flow in from neighbouring states, including Belarus, which regulate water levels on their own terms.
Bukantis, meanwhile, flags a different concern: pollution. As water volumes fall, he explains, pollutant concentrations rise, triggering algal blooms that pose a serious threat to aquatic ecosystems.
"This is the core problem – when untreated wastewater is discharged, and some smaller towns have no treatment facilities at all, phosphorus and nitrogen compounds build up and you get overgrowth, eutrophication [algal blooms]. This happens in lakes as well as rivers. The first line of defence would be better, more widespread wastewater treatment. If less pollution reaches our rivers, that alone would make a real difference," he said.

After the shooting, hundreds of students were evacuated from the school building to a safe location. The school is located on the university campus but has a separate secured area.
Police are establishing the circumstances of the shooting
Several hours after the incident, police said that the situation was under control. Parents and guardians of the students were urged to remain calm and follow the school administration’s instructions for picking up their children.
Authorities are currently establishing the circumstances of the incident. Police will provide verified information if necessary and urge the public to refrain from sharing unconfirmed reports, photographs or videos that could cause undue concern
He added that the safety and well-being of the school community remain a priority for law enforcement.
The shooting occurred after three high school students were killed and at least 20 people were injured in another attack in downtown Tacloban in June. After that, police said they were strengthening security at schools across the country.
In the Philippines, crimes involving firearms are common, in particular because of the illegal circulation of weapons; however, school shootings are relatively rare.

Judge blocks Trump administration's attempt to scrap move to Biden-selected FBI headquarters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:47:14 UTC
13:47:14 KST

Officials in the Trump administration sought to scrap plans for relocation to a site approved under the Biden administration in favour of repurposing another building just blocks from the current FBI headquarters in the nation’s capital.
A US judge on Monday blocked plans to move the FBI's headquarters to a federal office building in Washington, finding that President Donald Trump's administration illegally tossed out a previously approved plan to build a new facility nearby in Maryland.
The ruling is the latest development in a years-long battle over where to house the main office for the nation's premier law enforcement agency.
A site in Greenbelt, Maryland, was selected during former President Joe Biden's tenure, but Trump appointees sought to reverse that decision last year in favour of repurposing the Ronald Reagan Building, a federal office complex a few blocks from the FBI's existing headquarters.
US District Judge Theodore D. Chuang, an appointee of President Barack Obama, ruled that the move was “not in accordance with law,” and blocked the Trump administration from moving the FBI to the Reagan building, renovating it for the FBI or repurposing funds.
“This is not the first time courts have tried to undermine the administration in its goal to make government more cost-effective for American taxpayers,” the FBI said in a statement.
“The court has chosen to impermissibly intervene for political reasons. This FBI is mission focused and will continue the best course of action to meet the needs of law enforcement.” The suit was brought by the state of Maryland and Prince George's County.
“Maryland and Prince George’s County committed more than a decade of work to earn the FBI headquarters and pledged hundreds of millions of dollars," Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, a Democrat, said in a statement.
“By blocking the Trump Administration’s unlawful attempt to move the FBI to the Reagan Building and divert the funds Congress set aside for this project, the Court has cleared the path back to Greenbelt.”
Maryland Governor Wes Moore, also a Democrat, said, "Now it is time to stop the games and get to work building the world-class FBI headquarters that our public servants deserve, where it belongs: in Prince George’s County, Maryland.”
The FBI's current Pennsylvania Avenue headquarters, the J. Edgar Hoover Building, was dedicated in 1975. Proponents of moving the headquarters have said the brutalist-style building, where nets surround the facility to protect pedestrians from falling debris, has fallen into disrepair.
The Maryland location was selected over nearby Virginia following an intense competition between the two states.

====================================================================================================

Permafrost thaw threatens a rockslide above a Swiss village
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:46:03 EEST
13:46:03 KST

Permafrost thaw threatens a rockslide above a Swiss village
Kyiv • UNN
The village of Kandersteg is under threat of a landslide due to the unstable Spitze Stein rock, whose condition is deteriorating because of permafrost thaw. Residents are not afraid, as the authorities have taken precautionary measures.
The Swiss village of Kandersteg is facing the threat of a massive landslide due to the unstable Spitze Stein mountain formation, whose condition is deteriorating amid the thawing of permafrost and changes in glacier dynamics. The Associated Press reports, UNN writes.
Details
About 1,300 people live in Kandersteg, located in the canton of Bern. The Spitze Stein mountain formation is situated above the village and could trigger a significant landslide into the valley.
Scientists link the rising risk of such events to increasing temperatures. Permafrost contains frozen soil and rocks that help stabilize mountain slopes. When the ice melts, the rocks lose some of this support.
There is a lot of ice in the mountains and among the unconsolidated debris. When this ice melts, it acts like cement. These mountain slopes will become increasingly unstable
The Alps are facing growing risks
In May 2025, a massive landslide occurred in the neighboring Lötschental valley. A huge mass of rock and ice descended from the mountain and covered a significant part of the village of Blatten, which had been evacuated beforehand due to the threat of a collapse.
Residents of Kandersteg emphasize that their situation differs from what happened in Blatten. According to them, the authorities took the necessary measures in advance, and falling rocks from Spitze Stein have been observed for many years.
You know that this is happening, but you are not afraid
Another local resident, Rudolf Isler, also said that he did not consider the situation an immediate threat to the village.
This is not the same as in Blatten. It is a different situation. We are not afraid of the Spitze Stein rock formation. We have been seeing rocks fall from there for many years. The problem here is global warming and rising temperatures

Taiwan property administration uses drones to survey government land
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:41:00 UTC
13:41:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Finance's National Property Administration said on Monday that recent amendments allow the use of aerial drones instead of inspectors to survey state-owned real estate, according to a property administration press release.
The property administration said that after amendments to procedures on Aug. 4, aerial drone imagery may be overlaid on cadastral maps instead of sending surveyors to do on-site inspections. It said this method shortens the process and now includes land lease applications by state-owned and public utilities, including telecommunications and energy firms, improving efficiency.
A cadastral land survey defines and records a parcel of land's legal boundaries, dimensions, and ownership. The land is typically shown connected by physical boundary markers on its transcript.
The administration said the change mainly applies to the large number of lease-management and lease-renewal applications. It explained that on-site surveys for every case would delay other ones.
The administration said those properties typically have survey records that can be compared with recent aerial imagery to determine if there are violations. It said surveys will only be required if the condition of the on-site structure cannot be verified, allowing inspectors to prioritize other cases.
The administration said the revision excludes surveys of state-owned or public enterprises, including telecommunications firms and natural gas providers. It cited Taipower, which applied under the Electricity Act and submitted maps and other supporting documents in advance.
The administration said that river zones transferred with approval by the finance ministry may also be exempt with documentation. It said this is to save manpower and accelerate the application process.

Hsiao made the remarks while delivering the opening address at the Taiwan AI Academic Annual Conference, hosted by Academia Sinica. "AI cannot function without Taiwanese chips," Hsiao said, adding that the country's expertise across many applications and industries makes its contributions to the world irreplaceable.
On data governance and sovereign AI, Hsiao said AI models cannot function effectively without sufficient data. She noted that the Cabinet has established a sovereign AI and data governance framework to inventory and release AI-ready data that aligns with Taiwanese values.
Hsiao also warned about the risks associated with AI, saying that without the ability to prevent the mass production of misinformation, deepfakes, and cognitive warfare, or to defend critical infrastructure against cyberattacks, even the most advanced technology could become a double-edged sword that erodes social trust and democracy.
She said this is why President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has emphasized resilience in information, communications, and infrastructure. The government has also proposed an AI Basic Act to promote balanced innovation and security while promoting the development of human-centered and trustworthy AI, Hsiao said.
The vice president said she has attended the conference for three consecutive years, adding that the rapid pace of technological development has provided new lessons and areas for study each year. Hsiao said the government is deeply concerned about balanced development across industries and the country to ensure that the benefits of technological progress are shared broadly, per CNA.
Hsiao concluded by saying Taiwan is more than semiconductors and IT hardware, describing the country as a place where AI innovation can flourish. She called on industry, government, academia, and research institutions to continue promoting dialogue and cooperation so that AI can help Taiwan reach new heights.

Taiwan power suppliers prepare for Nvidia’s 800VDC architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:40:55 UTC
13:40:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s major power suppliers are developing products based on Nvidia’s 800VDC architecture as the new power standard moves toward commercial deployment, CTEE reported.
800VDC, or 800-volt direct current, is emerging as a key power standard for next-generation AI data centers. Current AI server power systems typically require electricity from the grid to undergo multiple conversions from alternating current to direct current before reaching individual racks, resulting in energy losses and generating additional heat, according to Business Next and UDN.
Distributing electricity as DC from an earlier stage can reduce the number of conversions and improve power efficiency. More than 80 equipment manufacturers and infrastructure providers are already developing products based on Nvidia’s specifications, indicating that an 800VDC supply chain is gradually taking shape.
Among Taiwan’s suppliers, Delta Electronics has already entered mass production of high-voltage direct current products. Shipments of its ±400VDC and 800VDC systems are scheduled to begin in the third quarter.
Overall volumes are expected to remain limited this year, with ±400VDC products accounting for a larger share through the end of the year. Shipments of 800VDC systems will depend on the rollout of Nvidia’s new platforms and the pace at which major cloud service providers adopt the architecture. More substantial growth is not expected until next year.
Lite-On Technology Corp. is also preparing its 800VDC power racks for the emerging architecture and is currently validating the products. The company has begun sending initial samples to customers and original design manufacturers, as well as conducting internal testing.
A second round of samples and customer integration testing is planned for October. If both certification stages proceed as scheduled, small-scale mass production could begin as early as November.
Lite-On expects to start larger-scale shipments in the first quarter of next year. One of its facilities in Kaohsiung will initially handle validation and production, while a US customer is expected to begin mass production with the products in the second quarter.
Nvidia plans to introduce the architecture in stages. The first phase, an 800VDC power rack compatible with Nvidia’s MGX platform, is scheduled to launch in the second half of this year and can be integrated with existing facilities.
Next year, the company plans to introduce power centers capable of supplying multiple server racks. Its longer-term goal is to develop facility-level DC power modules capable of converting grid electricity directly into 800VDC.

Judge blocks Trump administration's attempt to scrap move to Biden-selected FBI headquarters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:47:14 UTC
13:47:14 KST

Officials in the Trump administration sought to scrap plans for relocation to a site approved under the Biden administration in favour of repurposing another building just blocks from the current FBI headquarters in the nation’s capital.
A US judge on Monday blocked plans to move the FBI's headquarters to a federal office building in Washington, finding that President Donald Trump's administration illegally tossed out a previously approved plan to build a new facility nearby in Maryland.
The ruling is the latest development in a years-long battle over where to house the main office for the nation's premier law enforcement agency.
A site in Greenbelt, Maryland, was selected during former President Joe Biden's tenure, but Trump appointees sought to reverse that decision last year in favour of repurposing the Ronald Reagan Building, a federal office complex a few blocks from the FBI's existing headquarters.
US District Judge Theodore D. Chuang, an appointee of President Barack Obama, ruled that the move was “not in accordance with law,” and blocked the Trump administration from moving the FBI to the Reagan building, renovating it for the FBI or repurposing funds.
“This is not the first time courts have tried to undermine the administration in its goal to make government more cost-effective for American taxpayers,” the FBI said in a statement.
“The court has chosen to impermissibly intervene for political reasons. This FBI is mission focused and will continue the best course of action to meet the needs of law enforcement.” The suit was brought by the state of Maryland and Prince George's County.
“Maryland and Prince George’s County committed more than a decade of work to earn the FBI headquarters and pledged hundreds of millions of dollars," Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown, a Democrat, said in a statement.
“By blocking the Trump Administration’s unlawful attempt to move the FBI to the Reagan Building and divert the funds Congress set aside for this project, the Court has cleared the path back to Greenbelt.”
Maryland Governor Wes Moore, also a Democrat, said, "Now it is time to stop the games and get to work building the world-class FBI headquarters that our public servants deserve, where it belongs: in Prince George’s County, Maryland.”
The FBI's current Pennsylvania Avenue headquarters, the J. Edgar Hoover Building, was dedicated in 1975. Proponents of moving the headquarters have said the brutalist-style building, where nets surround the facility to protect pedestrians from falling debris, has fallen into disrepair.
The Maryland location was selected over nearby Virginia following an intense competition between the two states.

Permafrost thaw threatens a rockslide above a Swiss village
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:46:03 EEST
13:46:03 KST

Permafrost thaw threatens a rockslide above a Swiss village
Kyiv • UNN
The village of Kandersteg is under threat of a landslide due to the unstable Spitze Stein rock, whose condition is deteriorating because of permafrost thaw. Residents are not afraid, as the authorities have taken precautionary measures.
The Swiss village of Kandersteg is facing the threat of a massive landslide due to the unstable Spitze Stein mountain formation, whose condition is deteriorating amid the thawing of permafrost and changes in glacier dynamics. The Associated Press reports, UNN writes.
Details
About 1,300 people live in Kandersteg, located in the canton of Bern. The Spitze Stein mountain formation is situated above the village and could trigger a significant landslide into the valley.
Scientists link the rising risk of such events to increasing temperatures. Permafrost contains frozen soil and rocks that help stabilize mountain slopes. When the ice melts, the rocks lose some of this support.
There is a lot of ice in the mountains and among the unconsolidated debris. When this ice melts, it acts like cement. These mountain slopes will become increasingly unstable
The Alps are facing growing risks
In May 2025, a massive landslide occurred in the neighboring Lötschental valley. A huge mass of rock and ice descended from the mountain and covered a significant part of the village of Blatten, which had been evacuated beforehand due to the threat of a collapse.
Residents of Kandersteg emphasize that their situation differs from what happened in Blatten. According to them, the authorities took the necessary measures in advance, and falling rocks from Spitze Stein have been observed for many years.
You know that this is happening, but you are not afraid
Another local resident, Rudolf Isler, also said that he did not consider the situation an immediate threat to the village.
This is not the same as in Blatten. It is a different situation. We are not afraid of the Spitze Stein rock formation. We have been seeing rocks fall from there for many years. The problem here is global warming and rising temperatures

Taiwan property administration uses drones to survey government land
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:41:00 UTC
13:41:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Finance's National Property Administration said on Monday that recent amendments allow the use of aerial drones instead of inspectors to survey state-owned real estate, according to a property administration press release.
The property administration said that after amendments to procedures on Aug. 4, aerial drone imagery may be overlaid on cadastral maps instead of sending surveyors to do on-site inspections. It said this method shortens the process and now includes land lease applications by state-owned and public utilities, including telecommunications and energy firms, improving efficiency.
A cadastral land survey defines and records a parcel of land's legal boundaries, dimensions, and ownership. The land is typically shown connected by physical boundary markers on its transcript.
The administration said the change mainly applies to the large number of lease-management and lease-renewal applications. It explained that on-site surveys for every case would delay other ones.
The administration said those properties typically have survey records that can be compared with recent aerial imagery to determine if there are violations. It said surveys will only be required if the condition of the on-site structure cannot be verified, allowing inspectors to prioritize other cases.
The administration said the revision excludes surveys of state-owned or public enterprises, including telecommunications firms and natural gas providers. It cited Taipower, which applied under the Electricity Act and submitted maps and other supporting documents in advance.
The administration said that river zones transferred with approval by the finance ministry may also be exempt with documentation. It said this is to save manpower and accelerate the application process.

Hsiao speaks at Taiwan AI Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:40:59 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Tuesday that Taiwan's role in AI extends beyond its world-leading semiconductor industry, highlighting the country's expertise in cybersecurity, resilient systems, and AI applications, per CNA.
Hsiao made the remarks while delivering the opening address at the Taiwan AI Academic Annual Conference, hosted by Academia Sinica. "AI cannot function without Taiwanese chips," Hsiao said, adding that the country's expertise across many applications and industries makes its contributions to the world irreplaceable.
On data governance and sovereign AI, Hsiao said AI models cannot function effectively without sufficient data. She noted that the Cabinet has established a sovereign AI and data governance framework to inventory and release AI-ready data that aligns with Taiwanese values.
Hsiao also warned about the risks associated with AI, saying that without the ability to prevent the mass production of misinformation, deepfakes, and cognitive warfare, or to defend critical infrastructure against cyberattacks, even the most advanced technology could become a double-edged sword that erodes social trust and democracy.
She said this is why President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has emphasized resilience in information, communications, and infrastructure. The government has also proposed an AI Basic Act to promote balanced innovation and security while promoting the development of human-centered and trustworthy AI, Hsiao said.
The vice president said she has attended the conference for three consecutive years, adding that the rapid pace of technological development has provided new lessons and areas for study each year. Hsiao said the government is deeply concerned about balanced development across industries and the country to ensure that the benefits of technological progress are shared broadly, per CNA.
Hsiao concluded by saying Taiwan is more than semiconductors and IT hardware, describing the country as a place where AI innovation can flourish. She called on industry, government, academia, and research institutions to continue promoting dialogue and cooperation so that AI can help Taiwan reach new heights.

Taiwan power suppliers prepare for Nvidia’s 800VDC architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:40:55 UTC
13:40:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s major power suppliers are developing products based on Nvidia’s 800VDC architecture as the new power standard moves toward commercial deployment, CTEE reported.
800VDC, or 800-volt direct current, is emerging as a key power standard for next-generation AI data centers. Current AI server power systems typically require electricity from the grid to undergo multiple conversions from alternating current to direct current before reaching individual racks, resulting in energy losses and generating additional heat, according to Business Next and UDN.
Distributing electricity as DC from an earlier stage can reduce the number of conversions and improve power efficiency. More than 80 equipment manufacturers and infrastructure providers are already developing products based on Nvidia’s specifications, indicating that an 800VDC supply chain is gradually taking shape.
Among Taiwan’s suppliers, Delta Electronics has already entered mass production of high-voltage direct current products. Shipments of its ±400VDC and 800VDC systems are scheduled to begin in the third quarter.
Overall volumes are expected to remain limited this year, with ±400VDC products accounting for a larger share through the end of the year. Shipments of 800VDC systems will depend on the rollout of Nvidia’s new platforms and the pace at which major cloud service providers adopt the architecture. More substantial growth is not expected until next year.
Lite-On Technology Corp. is also preparing its 800VDC power racks for the emerging architecture and is currently validating the products. The company has begun sending initial samples to customers and original design manufacturers, as well as conducting internal testing.
A second round of samples and customer integration testing is planned for October. If both certification stages proceed as scheduled, small-scale mass production could begin as early as November.
Lite-On expects to start larger-scale shipments in the first quarter of next year. One of its facilities in Kaohsiung will initially handle validation and production, while a US customer is expected to begin mass production with the products in the second quarter.
Nvidia plans to introduce the architecture in stages. The first phase, an 800VDC power rack compatible with Nvidia’s MGX platform, is scheduled to launch in the second half of this year and can be integrated with existing facilities.
Next year, the company plans to introduce power centers capable of supplying multiple server racks. Its longer-term goal is to develop facility-level DC power modules capable of converting grid electricity directly into 800VDC.

Zamboanga city’s mayor, Khymer Adan Olaso, told radio station DZMM the shooter “managed to enter carrying a high-powered firearm and a .45 caliber pistol”.
“In the video, we see that he first shot at the teacher who was sitting at a table,” Olaso said, referencing a video being circulated by local media.
“It seems he missed, then moved to another room ... he shot another student there, the one who fell. It seems two others were also injured, probably before he killed himself.”
A video, circulated by local media, was seemingly live-streamed on Facebook.
The school separately confirmed there had been two fatalities.
The university president, Ernald Andal, confirmed there was no longer an active shooting and no additional fatalities or reported injuries.
Andal said the university was coordinating with authorities and would provide more details as information became available. “We do not want any of these things to happen. We wish to prioritise the safety of all our students,” he said.
In a statement posted online, the Philippine president, Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr, said: “We grieve with the families and the entire [school] community over a tragedy that should never have happened.
“I have directed our law enforcement agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into this incident and to determine what more must be done to prevent another family, another school and another community from suffering the same grief.”
Tuesday’s shooting comes after an attack at a public high school in Tacloban City in June that saw three students killed and about 20 injured after two students opened fire on campus.
In response, the government banned an online game, Gorebox, after it was discovered at least one of the alleged shooters regularly played it.
But the department of education told a senate committee last month that more support was needed to prevent a “copycat phenomenon”, as more incidents of violence followed the shooting, including bomb threats, stabbing and the recovery of firearms and ammunition, local media reported.
South-east Asia is grappling with violence among high school students, with a 14-year-old boy in Thailand allegedly shooting his grandparents and then killing more people at his school earlier this month before turning the gun on himself.

On Channel Seven's Agenda Setters, former Port Adelaide star Kane Cornes spoke from "the football point of view" of the issue, saying the players' lack of consideration for their teammates "is what makes [him] so angry".
"This is where I get really angry from a football point of view," he said.
"When you're two weeks away from a finals series, when Dane Rampe has played in four losing grand finals and he's probably in bed at age 36 or at home right now going 'this is my last chance, I'm 36, I had a chance to finish second and host another home final, give myself one last chance at winning a premiership'.
"[Jake] Lloyd's played in four losing grand finals, Heeney himself has played in three. … You'd think it would mean a bit more to Isaac Heeney ... on the eve of a finals series and put your teammates and your team in jeopardy."
On Fox Footy, Melbourne great Garry Lyon said he did not want to "understate or downplay the seriousness of" the case, insisting he could "only really comment on the one side and that is football-related matters".
"The rest will sort themselves out and again that's not to dismiss all parties involved in this, so let's get that on the table," he said.
"What we can discuss is the ramifications from a football point of view and this is an unmitigated disaster for the Sydney Swans and for the game.
"Those pictures on the eve of the AFL finals series with plain clothes [police] and police cars outside a hotel room one week out from the finals series is an absolute disaster."
McCarthy, now a commentator for Seven and Triple M, said focusing on "the football consequences" for the team caused by any potential sanctions or distractions sent the wrong message, particularly to girls and women.
The former Lion, Saint and Hawk also took issue with Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich saying the club was "extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation".
"AFL players occupy positions of enormous influence. We celebrate them as role models when they do wonderful things in the community, we can't suddenly decide they're 'just footballers' when difficult questions about behaviour, attitudes towards women and culture arise," she wrote on Instagram.
"Language matters too. Players don't simply 'find themselves in situations'. Adults have agency and make choices. Whatever this investigation ultimately determines, our language shouldn't inadvertently remove that agency or responsibility."
Current GWS player and McCarthy's former AFLW teammate, Tilly Lucas-Rodd, praised the post, while Lion star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."
Loading...
The news about the Swans emerged two weeks after former AFL player-agent Ralph Carr was revealed as the "well-connected man" convicted of rape last month.
In the wake of that revelation, former player and Australian Football Hall of Fame member Sam Newman questioned the evidence in the case and said the victim "might have buyer's remorse".
McCarthy questioned how much the AFL was doing to truly engage and include women and girls in footy spaces if someone like Newman remained in the hall of fame.
"We should be asking serious questions about what and who we continue to celebrate as a league," she wrote.
"The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates. It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise.
"This isn't about declaring anyone guilty. That is for police and the courts. When women are potentially harmed, why are we so quick to focus on what it means for the men on the football field?"

US, Canada hold last-minute talks to stop 50% U.S. tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
04:23:03 UTC
13:23:03 KST

US, Canada hold last-minute talks to stop 50% U.S. tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States and Canada have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other interminably over sore spots like Canadian softwood lumber imports and U.S. access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow the two neighbors still managed to remain friends, allies — and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile U.S.-Canada border is undefended, and nearly 330,000 people and $2 billion dollars’ worth of goods cross it every day; 800,000 Canadians live in the United States.
President Donald Trump’s belligerent approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Trump has hit Canadian goods with tariffs — in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States — and has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America’s 51st state.
The Canadian public is fed up. A petition to expel the U.S. ambassador, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 218,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of having “normalized’’ Trump’s talk of annexing Canada, among other things.
Tension could hit new heights at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday if Trump goes ahead with his plan to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
As the deadline approaches, the two countries are seeking a truce that would avoid the new round of tariffs.
″We are negotiating,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Monday, speaking in French. “The negotiations are very intense and delicate. This is not the time to talk about negotiations in public.”
Looking for an off ramp
Nearly 72% of Canadian goods exports last year went to the United States. And the Trump administration might be wary of imposing a hefty new tariff — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — ahead of November’s midterm elections. American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
“I don’t think either side really wants these tariffs to come into effect,’’ said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official. “There’s a pretty strong push on both sides to find an off ramp here.’’
Majerus said the United States is aiming to get Canada to buy more U.S. military equipment, including F-35 fighters; to take part in Trump’s “Golden Dome’’ missile defense; and to give the United States more access to critical minerals, thereby reducing America’s reliance on tenuous supplies from geopolitical rival China.
The Canadians would like relief from U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum as well as softwood lumber, which America says receives unfair government subsidies.
Trump relies on Smoot-Hawley to go after Canada
Trump has made tariffs the centerpiece of his second-term economic agenda. Last year, he imposed double-digit import taxes on almost every country on earth, justifying them by declaring the longstanding U.S. trade deficit a national emergency. The Supreme Court in February ruled that he’d overstepped his authority, striking down those tariffs and setting the stage for the federal government to pay refunds to importers.
Trump immediately looked for other ways to rebuild his tariff wall. Last month, he imposed import taxes of 10% to 12.5% on 59 countries and the European Union — which together account for 99% of U.S. imports — for allegedly failing to have or to enforce restrictions on imports made from forced labor.
Then he reached back to the Great Depression to find a cudgel with which to whack Canada, one of his favorite targets.
Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose 50% tariffs on products that account for about 5% of Canadian exports to the United States.
Nearly a century ago, with the U.S. and world economies in collapse, Congress passed the 1930 tariff law, imposing hefty taxes on imports from around the world. Known as the Smoot-Hawley tariffs, for their congressional sponsors, they are notorious among economists and historians for limiting world commerce and making the Great Depression worse.
Section 338 tariffs have never been used before. U.S. trade negotiators traditionally have favored another tool, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 — the provision Trump invoked for last month’s forced-labor tariffs.
Section 338 authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 50% on imports from countries that have discriminated against U.S. businesses. Unlike Section 301 sanctions, no investigation is required. Nor is there any limit on how long the tariffs can stay in place.
In announcing the Section 338 tariffs, Trump claimed that Canada discriminates against American exports of autos, alcohol and cheese. Trump is angry because Canada and China were the only countries that punched back with retaliatory tariffs of their own when he slapped levies on their products last year.
“If a country retaliates against us, we’re obviously not going to tolerate that,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters Friday at the Iowa State Fair. “We’ll take action. My sense is the Canadians, they want to have a more conciliatory approach, but we’ll see.”
New leverage to renegotiate USMCA
The U.S. is renegotiating a North American trade pact — the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement — that Trump strong-armed America’s neighbors into accepting in his first term. The threat of Section 338 tariffs gives the United States leverage to seek fresh concessions from Ottawa.
“From Carney’s perspective, you need (USMCA) to be renegotiated,’' said Christopher Gundermann, fellow in the economics program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. ”You can’t renegotiate it with a massive trade war going on.’'
But the Canadian public’s furor over Trump’s policies may limit Carney’s ability to cut a deal. Canada could retaliate again if the new 50% tariffs take effect, potentially aggravating a trade fight.
Canada’s government “cannot look like it is simply caving to the Trump administration’s demands,’’ said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. “Making further concessions without getting something meaningful in exchange would probably lead to a strong backlash ... The risk is for the Carney government to make Canada look weak and, therefore, even more vulnerable to future trade and geopolitical bullying on the part of the Trump administration.”
Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister for U.S. trade, met with Greer on Monday. He was tight-lipped afterward.
“The work is continuing,’’ he said. “We continue to do our job.’’
____
Gillies reported from Toronto.

Opening arguments set to begin in Meta’s federal trial over child harms
Oakland, Calif. (AP) — Opening arguments are set to kick off Tuesday in a pivotal trial for Meta Platforms in a California federal court.
Attorneys general from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey are seeking extensive financial damages plus changes to how the company operates Facebook and Instagram. Twenty-nine states sued the tech giant in 2023 over child safety and privacy — the other 25 will go to trial later. The company also faces lawsuits in state courts.
The lawsuit accuses the social media giant of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly and deliberately designing features that get children addicted to its platforms. It also argues that Meta routinely collects data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent, in violation of federal law.
“This week, we’re in court with the largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history. We’ll show a jury that Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people because looking away was more profitable,” said Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman in a statement.
Meta said it believes it has a strong case.
“We are proud of our record in protecting teens on our platforms and the amount of effort that we’ve put into developing protections over the years, even before these cases were ever filed, and continuing to the present day. We look forward to showing the judge and the jury those facts in court,” the company said in a statement.
U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland will oversee the proceedings, which are expected to last six to eight weeks, with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other executives and former employees testifying. Gonzalez Rogers, appointed to the bench by President Barack Obama in 2011, has overseen a bevy of complex, high-profile cases involving Big Tech. These include Elon Musk’s lawsuit against OpenAI and its founders as well as Epic Games’ lawsuit against Apple over its app store.
The trial is the latest in an avalanche of lawsuits against Meta Platforms and other social media companies including Google’s YouTube, TikTok and Snap, over arguments that their platforms harm young people, illegally collect their data and are deliberately designed to addict them.
