Rain brings respite as Belgium wrestles massive wildfire
- Rain brought relief to firefighters battling Belgium's largest wildfire in a century, which has burned 3,000 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve near the German border.
- Around 500 firefighters, aided by aircraft and local farmers, are working to contain the fire amid difficult peatland terrain and dry, hot weather conditions.
- The wildfire caused evacuations, thick smoke affecting nearby regions, and highlights the impact of Europe's historic heatwave and drought on Belgium's environment and communities.
AI generated
ROBERTVILLE, Belgium - Much-needed rain brought some respite on Aug 17 to firefighters on their fourth day battling Belgium’s worst wildfire in a century, which has scorched vast expanses of nature reserve on the German border.
Europe has been swept by weeks of devastating wildfires fuelled by dry conditions and a historically hot summer that has already contributed to the deaths of thousands of people.
France, Greece, Portugal and Spain were also battling major fires over the weekend.
In Belgium, currently the continent’s most urgent fire front, around 500 firefighters and emergency crews have mobilised to contain the blaze, which broke out on Aug 14 for reasons still unknown in the High Fens park, an area of boggy peatlands, pine forests and hiking trails.
Water-bombing aircraft and farmers’ tractors have joined forces to help tame the fire, which as of Aug 16 had spread to 3,000ha – an area half the size of Manhattan.
But Tony Hosmans, a crisis management spokesman, told reporters on Aug 17 the blaze was no longer advancing towards the German border – after creeping nearer over the weekend, prompting an evacuation order in the border town of Monschau.
The rain falling on Aug 17 on the area – with more forecast on and off throughout the week – was a welcome development.
“The wind is favourable, and the current rainfall is helping to contain the spread” of the fire, said Hosmans.
“At present, the fire is contained wherever intervention is possible,” he said – although he cautioned it had not yet been brought under control, with an aerial reconnaissance mission due to deliver a fuller picture later in the day.
The blaze broke out in an area that was ravaged by massive fires in 1911, during a similar period of heatwaves and drought.
It is the country’s largest wildfire since.
A huge area at the border has been blanketed by a thick plume of yellowish smoke, with fumes detected as far as eastern France, where authorities issued an air-pollution alert.
The smoke hazard has triggered the evacuation of two Belgian villages, whose residents were still under instruction to stay away.
‘Happening to us’
On-site operations have been made much harder by the fens’ terrain – a patchwork of heath, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy vehicles risk sinking into the ground, and firefighters struggle to tackle the fire at close range.
They have been counting heavily on aerial assistance to bring the situation under control, with two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden and two Dutch military Chinook helicopters backing up two Belgian helicopters on site.
Local farmers have also poured in to help battle the blaze, with a ballet of tractors pulling in tankers of water drawn from a nearby lake.
“We’ve provided drinks and some meals,” Annick Dodemont, who runs one of many local businesses supporting the firefighting operation, told AFP.
“We can’t go up there ourselves, so we help however we can,” said the 41-year-old.
Like much of Europe, Belgium has experienced a new spell of intense heat and drought in recent days.
Temperatures reached as high as 37 deg C in some parts of the country on Aug 14, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.
“It’s pretty shocking,” Dodemont said from her restaurant in Eupen. “You always think it happens somewhere else. Well, not anymore. It’s happening to us.” AFP

Congress MP Imran Masood refuses to sing Vande Mataram
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Imran Masood on Monday said that he would respect the national song but would not sing it, citing his constitutional right to practise his religion.His statement came amid row over the recitation of Vande Mataram involving grand old party high-command Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge.
While speaking on the Vande Mataram row, Masood told news agency ANI, "I cannot worship anyone except Allah. This right has been bestowed on me by the Constitution. You cannot snatch away this right from me. But, I won't insult it (Vande Mataram). I won't sing it but I will rise for it..."The Congress MP said he had never sung Vande Mataram and would not do so in the future, but would stand when it is recited."Go ahead and promote Vande Mataram if you want to. What difference does it make to me? I will do only as much as I want to, and I will do that. I have never sung it before, and I will not sing it in the future either. I will simply stand up. I have the constitutional right to follow my religion. First, read the complete history of Vande Mataram. Then come and talk to me. Read about where it came from, how it was written, and why it was written. Read the entire history first; after that, I will explain it to you..." Masood told IANS.The remarks came after the BJP lodged a complaint against former Congress president Sonia Gandhi over the Vande Mataram row.

US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to push a 15-point Gaza plan Israel has rejected.
The meeting on Monday comes a day after Kushner’s visit to El-Alamein, Egypt, to convene with Qatari, Turkish and Egyptian mediators. He was accompanied by Board of Peace Director-General Nickolay Mladenov and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair.

Kushner also held a rare meeting with members of the Hamas group’s political leadership, “with the objective of translating the roadmap’s obligations into concrete, verifiable steps”, an official familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera.
In late July, Trump said an agreement had been reached for the disarmament of Hamas. The deal was credited to the US-led Board of Peace, inaugurated in February 2026 and including roughly 40 countries – including Israel and several Arab states, though no Palestinian representatives – with Trump installed as its chair for life.

Several devotees were reportedly injured after a stampede-like situation broke out near temple complex
NEW DELHI: Several devotees were reportedly injured after a stampede-like situation broke out near the Mahakaleshwar Temple complex in Madhya Pradesh's Ujjain on Monday, amid a massive crowd gathered for Nag Panchami and Sawan Somvar.The incident was reported near Harsiddhi Chauraha after a rumour about electric current in barricades triggered panic among devotees heading towards the Shri Nagchandreshwar Temple, according to ANI. Some barricades reportedly broke as the crowd surged, leaving several devotees injured.The injured were taken to Charak Hospital for treatment, while Ujjain Collector and Superintendent of Police reached the spot and took charge of the situation.However, the temple administration denied that any chaos or stampede had occurred inside the temple and said devotees were continuing to have darshan without disruption.Temple administration denies stampedeMahakal Temple administrator Pratham Kaushik told ANI that darshan at the Nagchandreshwar Temple was continuing smoothly despite the unusually large crowd."On the occasion of Nag Panchami, darshan at Nag Chandreshwar Mandir at Shri Mahakaleshwar Mandir is continuously going on...So,

He came under a barricade when he was going for a darshan at Nath Chandreshwar Mandir. A stampede had broken out there. Nobody helped him. After seven to eight hours, I reached Harsiddhi Chauraha. We stood there for two hours. The crowd was swelling and since it was time for the aarti, we were stopped there. 08:07:51 UTC
17:07:51 KST

Myanmar junta chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing left for Russia on Monday for his first official visit to the country since he assumed the presidency in April, according to state media.
Russia will be the fifth country Min Aung Hlaing has visited since becoming president, with official trips to India, China, Laos, and, earlier this month, Thailand.
The former general is the subject of a raft of Western sanctions and has been on a quest for international legitimacy since winning a vote in parliament to become president, which came after an election dominated by an army-backed party in the absence of a viable opposition.
Min Aung Hlaing made four visits to Russia as junta chief, the first in June 2021 to attend a security conference, five months after seizing power in a coup. He visited twice in 2022 and again in March 2025, when he held formal talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Russia is hoping to open up opportunities in Myanmar for its energy companies. The two countries signed an agreement to construct a small-scale nuclear power plant in Myanmar when Min Aung Hlaing met Putin in 2025.
Russia, Myanmar strengthening defense ties
Russia and Myanmar signed a memorandum on investment cooperation for the strategically located Dawei Special Economic Zone in February 2025, including the construction of a port and an oil refinery.
Min Aung Hlaing's latest trip includes a Myanmar-Russia business forum. Joining him will be the chief minister of the Tanintharyi region, where Dawei is located, and the head of Myanmar's aerospace agency, according to state media.
Defense ties have grown in recent years, with Moscow providing army training and university scholarships to thousands of Myanmar soldiers, as well as selling arms to a military blacklisted by some Western countries.
Russia also said earlier this year that it would help train Myanmar's first cosmonaut.

Likud internal primaries begin as tensions continue over Netanyahu's expanded slate controls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:07:26 UTC
17:07:26 KST

The Likud Party closed its polling stations for its internal primaries on Monday evening after approximately 140,000 registered members were eligible to vote for candidates seeking spots on the party’s Knesset slate ahead of the October 27 elections.
The primaries came amid fierce internal tensions over changes that have expanded chairman Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s control over the party’s Knesset slate, which have made the primaries more competitive than in past years.
The voter turnout reached 53.5%, with 76,068 party members voting in the primaries, up about ten percentage points from the primaries held four years ago, taking into account the difference in voting hours, the Likud stated.
The results are expected to be announced late on Monday night.
Candidates who receive realistic slots on the list could hold significant roles in the government if Netanyahu is to be elected as prime minister in the October 27 election.
The polling began at 10 a.m. and continued until 9 p.m. at stations throughout the country.
The over 100 candidates seeking to secure a slot on the party's list continued to campaign throughout the morning. Many posted pictures of themselves with Netanyahu, such as Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, who is expected to receive a high slot on the list.
Regional Cooperation Minister David Amsalem posted a photo of himself voting, calling on registered members to join.
"I believe in Likud members, in their wisdom, their hearts, and in our path. We did our part with great love. Now I call on everyone who has not yet voted: Get out of the house, go to the polls, and make your voice heard," he stated.
Likud ministers and members of Knesset running in the primaries also continued throughout the day to photograph themselves casting their ballots at the various voting stations throughout the country.
Regional Cooperation Minister David Amsalem posted a photo of himself voting, calling on registered members to join.
"I believe in Likud members, in their wisdom, their hearts, and in our path. We did our part with great love. Now I call on everyone who has not yet voted: Get out of the house, go to the polls, and make your voice heard," he stated.
Parties not required to hold primaries, Likud holds votes
Netanyahu showed up at the Jerusalem polling station at the International Convention Center (ICC) to vote in the afternoon.
He stated on Sunday ahead of the primaries that he would join the voting and cast his ballot “for a winning slate.”
“I trust you, Likud members, to choose your representatives correctly, according to your own judgment. I am not interfering in the national list, and I wish everyone success,” Netanyahu added.
Agriculture and Food Security Minister Avi Dichter told The Jerusalem Post, while at the ICC in Jerusalem to cast his vote, that this year’s primaries had generated a different level of enthusiasm, with turnout among members appearing “higher and stronger,” and voters arriving with “a wide smile on their face.”
Giving backing to the premier amid the tensions over the reserved slots, Dicter added that "we need to build a good team beside and behind Prime Minister Netanyahu."
It was later reported by Israeli media that haredi (ultra-Orthodox) activists had registered to the party ahead of the primaries to vote in favor of preferred candidates, despite not having a previous connection to the party.
Likud has for years prided itself on conducting primaries in which its registered members are eligible to vote for the Knesset list. Parties are not required to hold primaries in Israel, and only a few do so.
Netanyahu pushed to change the system in recent weeks ahead of the primaries, leading to an especially competitive race with even fewer slots available than usual.
Netanyahu was granted the authority to determine eight slots within the first 30 spots on the party list last month following a vote on the controversial decision by the Likud Central Committee.
There were reports that Netanyahu had threatened to leave Likud if the proposed changes were not advanced.
Those within the party who oppose changing the primaries have argued that it will cause those who would otherwise score highly in the primaries to fall further down the list.
The Likud primaries are further competitive because the party currently has around 40 ministers and MKs serving in the government and Knesset, but recent polls project the party winning only about 22 seats, leaving many at risk of losing their places on the party’s Knesset list.
Further tensions surrounding the slots also come after the Tel Aviv District Court last week rejected Likud MK Afif Abed’s attempt to restore a narrowly approved change allowing current and former MKs, ministers and deputy ministers to run in the party’s district primaries, leaving the restrictions in place ahead of the vote.
Likud had announced last week that one of Netanyahu’s first reserved slots would go to entrepreneur and businessman Oren Dobronsky.
Additional reserved slots were later granted by Netanyahu to three ministers: Defense Minister Israel Katz, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, and Likud Central Committee Chairman Haim Katz, who also holds multiple ministerial portfolios.
The party said its internal court ruled that the defense minister should receive a reserved slot in order to “allow him to focus on security needs rather than engage in politics at this time.”
Sa'ar to receive reserved slot as part of party merger
Likud also stated that Sa’ar would receive a reserved slot as part of the merger agreement between his party and Likud and that the Likud Central Committee chairperson would receive a slot due to his senior position in the party.
Sa’ar had announced in 2025 that his New Hope-United Right would be merging with Likud, and would be returning to the party. He previously resigned from Likud in 2020, heavily criticizing Netanyahu at the time.
The changes to the party’s primaries that have expanded Netanyahu’s control over the Knesset list have led to fierce internal tensions, with some party members in favor and others strongly against.
A fierce critic of changing the system has been MK Tally Gotliv, who is viewed as a candidate who would receive broad support from registered party members.
She claimed during the voting that there were polling stations with fake ballots that did not include her name.
"Stay alert. Likud activists and vote contractors are in a panic over the power of independent votes," she stated.
"Update me directly. A polling station with a fake ballot will be disqualified," she added.
Gotliv has sharply criticized the Tuesday decision to reserve the slots for the three ministers, condemning the defense minister.
She called the decision to grant the defense minister a reserved slot “a disgraceful move that mocks Likud voters."
Likud MK Amit Halevi, who has expressed support for allowing the premier to reserve slots, told the Post on Sunday that the primaries “will be a democratic celebration in the Likud.”
“I wish more parties conducted themselves democratically like the Likud. Some 140,000 members, active, engaged citizens who make their voices heard and have an influence, will go to the polls tomorrow,” he added.
The primaries determine the Likud’s Knesset slate, with the party chairman placed first. Registered members then vote for candidates on the national list, while members from geographic districts vote for candidates from their respective districts.
Candidates chosen on the national list are combined with district representatives and places that guarantee representation for groups including women, immigrants, young members, and minorities. The regulations also reserve certain positions for candidates chosen by the party chairman.
The precise locations of those different categories are determined before each election through the party’s temporary election regulations. That is why the current fight has centered not only on whether primaries will take place, but on how much of the resulting slate the members will actually control.
Other party leaders from Netanyahu's coalition expressed support for the primaries.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who leads the far-Right Otzma Yehudit Party, voiced his support for various Likud candidates, including Gotliv and Women's Advancement Minister May Golan.
The Religious Zionist Party, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, also expressed support.
"Good luck to all the candidates, and, God willing, success to all of us together in the upcoming elections," the party stated.
"The national camp must continue to lead Israel toward continued growth and prosperity," it added.
Democrats Party leader Yair Golan, from the oppostion bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu in the upcoming elections. sharply criticized the primaries.
"Never have so many people vied for a place on the deck of the Titanic," he stated.
Sam Halpern and Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

Qantas A380 flew to US and back with maintenance light left in wing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:04:52 UTC
17:04:52 KST

ATSB investigation finds maintenance light was left in Qantas A380 jet wing
In short:
A work light was left inside the wing of a Qantas A380, which flew multiple international trips before it was found.
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said it was due to a breakdown in processes at Qantas.
What's next?
Qantas has established a working group and changed its tool-control procedures.
A Qantas A380 was cleared to fly passengers return from Sydney to Dallas with a large maintenance light accidentally left inside its wing.
It follows a 2023 incident in which a large tool was left inside a Qantas A380 engine and was not recovered until multiple international trips had been completed.
An Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation found the 33 centimetre light was left behind after maintenance on the aircraft's air conditioning system in Sydney on January 7.
The aircraft then flew to Dallas-Fort Worth and back before maintenance staff realised the light was missing and recovered it from the wing two days later.
The ATSB's final report into the incident found that although the light did not cause any damage to the wing, foreign objects posed a "significant risk to the safe operation of an aircraft".
ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said the incident was due to a breakdown in tool accountability processes.
"Even well-established processes can be vulnerable when they rely solely on consistent human performance, particularly during maintenance tasks which are often conducted in challenging environments and under operational pressures," he said.
"Tool control systems and procedures must account for this variability with safeguards to detect and recover from errors."
The report said Qantas issued a safety directive to address changes to its tooling control processes and procedures and had also formed a "tooling working group".
Qantas said the light had no impact on the operation of the aircraft and it had voluntarily reported the incident to the ATSB.
"Since the event, we have strengthened our tool-control procedures, including introducing a mandatory pre-clearance check to confirm all tooling is accounted for following maintenance," a spokesperson said.
Second tool left inside Qantas A380
It is the second incident involving a tool being left in one of the airline's super jumbos.
In December 2023, a Qantas A380 flew multiple international trips before a 1.25 metre nylon turning tool was discovered in one of the plane's engines.
An ATSB report found maintenance staff "lost" the "turning tool" in an A380's outboard engine, and it was only discovered after it had been cleared for service, flying multiple trips between Australia and the US.
Last week, Qantas passengers in South Africa were left stranded in Johannesberg for three days after a problem with the nose wheel of an A380 saw their flight to Sydney cancelled.
Qantas sent another flight to bring the stranded passengers home.
CQUniversity aviation expert and associate professor Steven Leib said any unaccounted-for objects found inside an aircraft were "a real safety concern".
"It may not seem like a big deal, leaving a light or leaving a tool, but these are things that could move around during flight, which could jeopardise the safety of the flight," Dr Leib said.
However, he said the two incidents were not enough to suggest Qantas had a systemic problem.
"The discovery of the lost object was made by the accountability system," he said.
"They were able to trace when it was last used, when it was meant to have been returned and what work was being carried out."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung announced Monday that it has partnered with RAI Technology to deploy an AI-backed traffic monitoring system in busy areas, according to a city Transportation Bureau press release.
The Transportation Bureau signed a memorandum of understanding with RAI. The bureau said this marks a transition to active detection, real-time notification, and data-backed decision-making.
Transportation Bureau Director Yeh Chao-fu (葉昭甫) said the new system will reduce staff workload, as monitoring was previously done manually to verify accidents and traffic congestion. He noted that going through surveillance footage causes delays as responders await confirmation.

When vehicle queues reach a preset threshold, the system will generate a detailed report and notify traffic management staff to determine the appropriate response.
Yeh said the city will then target the entry and exit ramps of Provincial Highway 74 by using cameras at Huanzhong East Road and Taiyuan Road to assess traffic flow. The bureau will use collected statistics to determine the appropriate traffic control measures.
Yeh said the third pilot will take place during the Xinshe Flower Festival, where cameras will be set up at shuttle bus terminals. Once the queue reaches a preset threshold, the system will notify the bureau to respond accordingly.

Taiwan personnel agency rejects proposal to scrap National Travel Card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:02:00 UTC
17:02:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet's personnel administration rejected a proposal to end the National Travel Card program, saying it encourages civil servants to take annual leave and protects employee health, CNA reported Monday.
UDN reported that the proposal was posted on the government's Public Policy Network Participation Platform. It called for ending the card program and allowing unused leave to be fully compensated in cash when civil servants cannot take time off because of work demands.
The proposal said the current system requires part of the compensation linked to unused leave to be spent through the National Travel Card. It argued that restrictions on eligible purchases limit how civil servants can use the money.
In response, the personnel administration said it would not adopt the proposal for now. It said replacing the system with cash payments could give civil servants less incentive to take enough time off, per Up Media.
The agency said required leave days help protect employees' physical and mental health. Government figures show civil servants took an average of 11.32 days of annual leave in 2025.
Civil servants entitled to more than 10 days of annual leave are generally required to take at least 10 days. They can receive up to NT$16,000 (US$502) a year through the National Travel Card program, per Liberty Times.
Half of the subsidy can be spent without tourism-related restrictions. The other NT$8,000 must be used for tourism-related spending.
The personnel administration said the card subsidy is a welfare benefit rather than overtime pay or direct compensation for unused leave. Civil servants who cannot use all their annual leave because of work demands can still claim cash compensation for up to 20 unused days beyond the required 10 days.
The Cabinet has approved keeping the current rules from 2026 through 2028. The personnel administration said the program is generally reviewed every three years, per FTV News.
The National Travel Card program began in 2003 to encourage civil servants to take vacations and support domestic tourism. Critics say the program has since moved away from its original purpose.
Former Minister without Portfolio Chang Ching-sen (張景森), opposition lawmakers, and civil servant groups have called for changes to the system. Their proposals include easing spending restrictions, raising the subsidy, or replacing the card with cash payments.
Some civil servants also question whether the card still encourages tourism. They say the subsidy is often spent on hotel vouchers, meals, or everyday goods instead.

====================================================================================================

China’s passport warfare targets Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:01:57 UTC
17:01:57 KST

China is turning travel documents, overflight permits, visas, and border checkpoints into weapons in a quiet campaign to isolate Taiwan from the world.
In late April, Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar revoked overflight clearances for President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) planned flight to Eswatini under pressure from Beijing. Taipei and Mbabane outmaneuvered the blockade when King Mswati III’s aircraft transported the Taiwanese delegation on a much longer route through friendly airspace, landing safely in Eswatini on May 2.
By July, this containment campaign had begun targeting ordinary citizens. The Moroccan Embassy in Tokyo halted mandatory visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese tourists, forcing Taipei to respond with a reciprocal visa suspension against Moroccan nationals.
In August, Ugandan immigration officers at Entebbe International Airport withheld Taiwanese passports and demanded that Taiwanese travelers produce Chinese passports before their documents would be returned.
These shocks reveal a trend toward “passport warfare” — the weaponization of airspace, transit hubs, visas, and checkpoints to isolate Taiwan. This administrative containment mirrors the coercive diplomatic warfare the Chinese Communist Party aggressively conducts against countries that maintain official relations with Taiwan.
By forcing foreign states to deny transit, entry, or basic document recognition to Taiwanese passport holders, Beijing achieves through bureaucratic pressure what it cannot yet enforce through military might. The result directly undermines cross-strait deterrence and assurance.
The Zero-Tariff Cauldron
These travel restrictions reflect clear geopolitical patterns.
Sovereignty fears drive complete transit blockades in Georgia and Moldova, where governments fear legitimizing breakaway regions and have strong reasons to please Beijing. Economic dependencies dictate entry bans in Venezuela and Azerbaijan, while Chinese investment in Morocco’s Tangier Tech Smart City forms part of the broader context for Rabat’s recent visa freeze.
Elsewhere, proxy disputes dictate borders, as Somalia has barred Taiwanese travelers in retaliation for Taipei’s ties with Somaliland.
This African containment stems from a unified economic carrot. On Feb. 14, during the 39th African Union Summit, Chinese leader Xi Jinping announced a unilateral zero-tariff policy for 53 African nations, effective May 1.
Eswatini, Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in Africa, was the sole African country excluded from Beijing’s duty-free umbrella.
In exchange, African leaders have increasingly aligned their borders and diplomatic language with Beijing. Recent joint declarations with hardline dependents such as Zimbabwe, Equatorial Guinea, Algeria, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have dropped historical language endorsing a peaceful resolution of cross-strait relations.
By stating only that Taiwan is an inalienable part of Chinese territory and omitting references to peace, these accords grant diplomatic cover to a future military blockade.
Deterrence, Assurance, and Silkworms
International relations theory holds that deterrence relies on raising the costs of aggression, while assurance guarantees that maintaining the status quo preserves security.
Beijing’s passport warfare subverts this balance through consular and airspace deterrence. It creates a gray-zone barrier to prove that standard travel can result in immediate logistical stranding.
This behavior embodies the Chinese idiom 蠶食鯨吞, or “to nibble away like a silkworm before swallowing like a whale.”
Avoiding hot war, Beijing relies on the silkworm’s patience. It pressures civil aviation systems, border authorities, and travel-document databases to make Taiwanese mobility appear abnormal, disputed, and administratively inconvenient.
Squeezing access in isolated hubs gradually conditions the world to accept Taiwan’s isolation. Once this erasure is normalized, the strategy can shift to the whale’s swallow: collapsing status quo assurances and eliminating Taiwan’s international presence entirely.
The Expanding Gray-Zone Grid
This containment has expanded beyond historic non-recognition blocks, combining passport warfare and legal pressure into a unified lawfare campaign.
In South Africa, Pretoria excluded Taiwan from its automated e-visa platform and demanded that Taiwan move its liaison office from Pretoria to Johannesburg, treating travel access and representation as concessions to Beijing.
In China’s own legal system, the CCP has expanded extraterritorial threats. Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has raised concerns over Article 63 of China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which targets overseas organizations and individuals accused of undermining ethnic unity or promoting separatism.
At the same time, Chinese judicial guidelines on “Taiwan independence” have turned travel through China and China-aligned states into a growing risk for Taiwanese, overseas Taiwanese, and foreign supporters of Taiwan.
Thailand and South Korea have also intensified screening of Taiwanese arrivals under the pretext of fighting transnational fraud, demonstrating how ordinary border enforcement can be turned into broader friction against Taiwanese mobility.
Uganda’s August passport seizures show the campaign’s most blunt form. Ugandan immigration officers at Entebbe withheld Taiwanese passports, demanded Chinese passports, and in earlier cases detained or deported Taiwanese travelers.
Foreign nationals are not immune. Western and other foreign passport holders who renew documents through trade offices or de facto embassies in Taipei can face denial or heightened scrutiny at Chinese checkpoints when “Taipei” appears as the place of issue. In China’s political reading of travel documents, even a neutral administrative field can become a sovereignty trap.
The same pattern appears in paperwork erasure. Serbia and Bolivia process visas for Taiwanese on loose sheets of paper, while Jamaica requires travelers to purchase a separate affidavit of identity to avoid creating an official administrative record on a Taiwanese passport.
The September Entry and Exit Codes
The structural normalization of passport warfare is arriving through China’s sweeping new entry and exit regulation, State Council Decree No. 841, which takes effect Sept. 15.
The 19-article regulation gives Beijing broader administrative tools to refuse entry, cancel transit, restrict exit, demand supporting documents, require electronic data, and impose entry bans on people accused of violating vague border or national-security classifications.
This codifies a weapon-ready architecture for gray-zone border control.
Under the new regulation, border officers and visa authorities can demand documents, materials, and electronic data when verifying a traveler’s identity or stated purpose of travel. False materials or statements can be used to deny entry or exit documents, refuse entry, or impose bans of one to five years.
The system gives Beijing more tools to punish travelers whose identities, documents, political views, or links to Taiwan are deemed irregular.
Because Beijing routinely treats Taiwanese as Chinese citizens under its domestic administrative practices, these measures could be selectively applied to Taiwanese tech workers, academics, businesspeople, activists, and public figures traveling to or from China.
What appears to be a border-management rule is in practice another tool for ideological compliance.
The Democratic Counterstrike
To neutralize this strategy, Taiwan and its allies must establish diplomatic counter-deterrence.
First, democratic partners should impose immediate diplomatic costs on states that target Taiwanese travelers. Taiwan’s July 30 reciprocal visa suspension against Morocco offers a model.
If a state bans Taiwanese transit, withholds passports, or enforces discriminatory entry rules under Beijing’s pressure, the US, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, and other partners should respond with bureaucratic delays, reciprocal scrutiny, or restrictions on electronic visa access for that country’s officials.
Second, allies must mobilize multilateral aviation protections.
Beijing’s airspace coercion violates the apolitical spirit of the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation. Western allies should explicitly extend freedom-of-navigation principles to civil aviation by guaranteeing alternative routes, priority transit, diplomatic escorts, or emergency logistical support for Taiwanese officials facing blockade attempts.
Eswatini’s royal-jet intervention showed that Beijing’s airspace choke points can be broken. The democratic world should systematize that lesson before the next attempted blockade.
Third, allies should establish pre-cleared sovereign whitelisting.
The US, Canada, UK, and Schengen Area should integrate Taiwan into automated, depoliticized biometric corridors such as Global Entry, SmartGate, and similar trusted-traveler systems. Bypassing manual embassy checks protects travelers from localized diplomatic pressure.
This automation is urgent. As the Uganda passport seizures show, Taiwan often lacks local embassies and must route emergency support through remote offices, such as its representative office in Somaliland.
Automated and trusted systems would make Taiwan’s global mobility harder to break, even under China’s incoming Sept. 15 border rules.
A Global Blueprint for Erasure
Passport warfare is an existential threat disguised as paperwork.
The institutional foundations for this global containment were codified during the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation meeting in Beijing, where every participating African head of state except Eswatini declared support for China’s “national reunification” narrative and “all efforts by the Chinese government” to achieve the goal.
Driven by Beijing’s economic leverage, this language fuels the silkworm’s first nibble, expanding the blockade into a systemic global consular net.
In Southeast Asia, staunch Beijing allies such as Cambodia and Laos have weaponized visa infrastructure by tightening restrictions on Taiwanese nationals while offering broader entry privileges to Chinese citizens.
In South America, China has used expanded visa-waiver frameworks with core trade partners such as Brazil, Argentina, and Peru to encourage compliance with Beijing’s passport and sovereignty demands, increasingly choking off standard entry procedures for Taiwanese travelers.
Normalizing a world where autocrats dictate international transit does not prevent conflict. It accelerates the whale’s final swallow.
If the democratic world fails to break Beijing’s consular blockade today, its own freedom of movement will be held hostage tomorrow.

Streaming site pulls Chainsmoker Cat series in Hong Kong over breach of ad rules
Animation Crazy receives letter from Department of Health saying anime series flouts rules against advertising smoking products online
A Taiwan-based streaming platform has removed Japanese anime series Chainsmoker Cat for Hong Kong audiences because the programme is in breach of the city’s ban on online smoking advertisements.
Animation Crazy, a streaming platform launched by Bahamut, a Taiwanese internet forum and news website, said on Monday that it recently received a letter from Hong Kong’s Department of Health concerning Chainsmoker Cat.
The show’s content contravened rules that prohibited advertising smoking products on the internet under the Smoking (Public Health) Ordinance in Hong Kong, the platform cited the department as saying.
“To comply with local regulations and the requirements of Hong Kong’s Department of Health, we will suspend the broadcast of Chainsmoker Cat in the Hong Kong region immediately,” a social media post by the platform said.
“We deeply regret and apologise for this situation, and we offer our most sincere apologies to our users in Hong Kong.”
According to the ordinance, no one should place a smoking product advertisement on the internet, with offenders facing a HK$50,000 (US$6,370) fine upon summary conviction and a further HK$1,500 fine for each day the offence continues.

SC tells Karnataka to follow CWMA directions
The Supreme Court on Monday directed Karnataka to comply with the Cauvery Water Management Authority’s (CWMA) directions on the release of Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu.The court posted for hearing on August 24 Tamil Nadu’s plea seeking directions for the release of water.It said the matter could be taken up then, allowing an updated status on the water released by Karnataka to be placed before the court.Tamil Nadu approached the Supreme Court on August 3, saying it was not receiving its allocated share of Cauvery water despite the state facing a rain-deficient year.
The state government alleged that both the quantity recommended for release by the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee and the water actually supplied by Karnataka were well below its requirement.Also read: ‘Protect farmers, abide by law’: Karnataka CM Shivakumar on releasing Cauvery water to TNTamil Nadu said recent rainfall in the catchment areas of the KRS and Kabini reservoirs had increased the volume of water due to the state.According to the state government, the proportionate share due at Biligundlu should be 26.954 TMC.At a meeting on July 28, the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee directed Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days from July 29. Tamil Nadu, however, said the actual flow recorded at Biligundlu on the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border ranged between 158 and 550 cusecs from July 29 to August 2.
The state government also cited storage levels in Karnataka’s four reservoirs. As of August 3, the combined storage in the Krishna Raja Sagara, Kabini, Harangi and Hemavathy reservoirs stood at 77.537 TMC, according to a Tamil Nadu government statement.Tamil Nadu said the available storage indicated that Karnataka could release the state’s due share without difficulty.

Seoul responds to Trump&apos;s decision to scale back military exercises
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:39:44 EEST
16:39:44 KST

Seoul responds to Trump's decision to scale back military exercises
Kyiv • UNN
South Korea is reviewing Trump's comments about scaling back joint exercises, hoping for substantive negotiations. Pyongyang has not yet responded, while experts warn of possible high costs.
South Korea has issued a statement on US President Donald Trump's decision to reduce the annual military exercises between the two countries, UNN reports, citing the BBC.
Context
President Donald Trump said that the United States would "substantially reduce" joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. He also said on Truth Social that South Korea had recently refused to join the United States in the "denuclearization" of Iran. "These exercises are not only expensive, with a significant portion of the costs paid by the United States of America (as always!), but they also send an absolutely inappropriate and hostile signal," Trump wrote.
Seoul's response
Seoul said it was reviewing Trump's comments, adding that it hoped favorable relations between Washington and Pyongyang could lead to meaningful negotiations. Pyongyang has not yet commented on the situation.
South Korea earlier said that the exercises with the United States would continue "as scheduled".
This came after North Korea conducted tests of ballistic missiles banned by the United Nations this month.
Trump's statement came less than 24 hours after he posted an old photograph of himself and Kim from 2019, writing that they had been good friends, "despite the unfriendly look in this particular photo".
In its statement, South Korea's presidential Blue House said it would continue diplomatic consultations on military cooperation between the United States and Korea related to the Strait of Hormuz, and would also discuss details of joint military exercises with the United States.
Experts suggest that abandoning joint military exercises could result in high costs and relatively little benefit.
Last week, US and South Korean military leaders held a joint press conference at which they announced the "Ulchi Freedom Shield" exercises.
During the press conference, the military leaders also mentioned North Korea's deployment of troops to assist Russia's war against Ukraine.
US military spokesman Ryan Donald said that "our exercises take this threat into account," referring to North Korean soldiers returning from the battlefield. About 28,500 US servicemen are stationed in South Korea.
On Friday, North Korea's Foreign Ministry condemned the joint military exercises as a "rehearsal for an aggressive war".
The joint exercises took place several days after South Korea, the United States and Japan detected North Korea's second missile test in several days.
Pyongyang has accelerated efforts to expand its nuclear and missile programs following the failure in 2019 of Kim's high-profile diplomatic engagements with Trump during his first term in the White House.
He became the first sitting US president to set foot on North Korean territory when he visited it seven years ago.
For Seoul, Trump's post is an ambiguous signal. On the one hand, they had asked Trump to engage with Pyongyang, and the post raises hopes that he may bring Kim back to the negotiating table. But Trump also hints that he is dissatisfied with South Korea's unwillingness to make a direct military or logistical contribution to US military operations against Iran, the publication writes.
He also expressed dissatisfaction with other allies over their unwillingness to intervene in the conflict, including Japan, France and the United Kingdom.
Trump's move to reduce joint military exercises with South Korea is not unprecedented. He completely halted the exercises in 2018 during denuclearization talks with Kim. He said at the time that the annual exercises were "provocative" toward North Korea and that ending the "war games" would save the United States "a tremendous amount of money". The exercises were reduced again in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic.
What they say in Ukraine
Ukraine has also commented on Trump's decision regarding the exercises.
"At the same time, North Korea is sending military personnel to gain experience in Russia’s war against Ukraine, preparing for a possible escalation on the Korean Peninsula," Andriy Kovalenko, head of the National Security and Defense Council’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said on social media on Monday.

Traffic falls in Strait of Hormuz, say maritime monitors
Maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell last week, according to two maritime monitors, with no end in sight to the grinding conflict between Iran and the United States.
Crossings through the key waterway fell 19.5%, according to Marine Traffic and Kpler, declining from a high of 19 on Aug. 11 to just three on Aug. 16.
Of the total 95 crossings, 51 vessels used the route established by Iran, while 44 used other routes, according to Marine Traffic.
Traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, the gateway to the Red Sea, where Iranian-backed Houthi forces have attacked Saudi ships, increased slightly to 254, up from 238.
"Yet security conditions remain volatile," said Kpler. "Two attacks on 11 August resulted in six seafarer fatalities and 10 injuries, underscoring the gap between resilient traffic volumes and persistent regional risk."
Pentagon signs $22.9B deal for Tomahawk missiles amid reports of shortages

"Guaranteeing our naval and joint forces have the lethal firepower they need to deter aggression and protect the homeland is paramount," Cao said in a statement. "The Department is utilizing every available tool to meet the demands of our current operations."
An analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank released last month found that U.S. stocks of Patriot and THAAD air defense missiles have been slashed by the conflict with Iran.
Before it began in late February, the United States had more than 2,300 Patriot and more than 450 THAAD interceptors - figures that CSIS estimated have been roughly halved or more in the subsequent months of war.
The Washington Post reported this month that President Trump had demanded answers from Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth about munitions shortages at a recent cabinet meeting. Mr. Trump and Hegseth both later denied that the U.S. was faced with dwindling missile stocks.
Tomahawk missiles are mainly launched from submarines and warships and can travel more than 1,000 miles.

Yemen's Houthi rebels claim attack on Saudi military ship in Red Sea
Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis claimed Monday to have targeted a Saudi military vessel and four accompanying military vessels off the coast of Mokha, Saudi Arabia, in the Red Sea.
Houthi forces "managed to target a military landing ship belonging to the Saudi enemy, along with four accompanying military boats in the Red Sea off the coast of Mokha, using a number of ballistic missiles," Houthi military spokesperson Yehya Saree said in a post on X.
"The strike was accurate and direct, resulting in the complete burning of the ship, the sinking of a number of the boats, and the burning of the remainder," he added.
The Houthis said several weeks ago that they would enforce a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports. The two sides have been at war since 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war on the side of the Western-backed government, against the Houthis.
A ceasefire had been holding until last month, when the Houthis opened a new front in the regional war in support of their benefactor, Iran. Saudi forces last month joined with U.S. forces in airstrikes on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
Iran's vice president says internet censorship to end
Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said Monday that President Masoud Pezeshkian had decided the country's censorship of the internet should be brought to an end, although he said the process would take time due to the involvement of myriad legal bodies and councils.
Aref was quoted by the semi-official Tasnim News agency as saying the government considered improving the quality of Iranians' internet connectivity a priority, but he warned that Iran's enemies were seeking to use economic pressure to undermine social resilience.
He called on Iranian media to take a more assertive role in what he called a hybrid war, saying: "The media must shift from a defensive position to an offensive one; because in media work, the first narrator is the winner."
IRGC rejects Trump's claim of backchannel talks with U.S. as a "delusion"
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohbehi on Monday denied President Trump's claim that Washington was engaged in backchannel discussions with Iran's IRGC over the war.
"There are no talks taking place between IRGC officials and the Americans, and this lie by Trump is merely fantasies caused by the delusions and nightmares he has suffered as a result of defeat and desperation in the war," Mohbehi was quoted as saying by Iran's semi-official Tasnim News agency.
He said the IRGC "speaks its word on the battlefield," while "diplomatic matters fall within the remit of other parts of the Islamic Republic."
"According to the information we have and based on the statements of the respected officials of the Foreign Ministry, even in this area, no talks are currently taking place with the Americans because of their broken promises and the dark experience of repeated and continual U.S. breaches of commitments," insisted Mohbehi.
Iran's IRGC warns "strategic surprises" in store with shift to defense in "an offensive form"
A senior figure in Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Monday that the country's armed forces would adopt a more "offensive form" of defense amid the ongoing war with the U.S.
Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani, the political deputy of the IRGC, told Iran's Fars News agency that the armed forces would adopt a "transformative" approach under its recently refreshed leadership, including a potential shift toward more offensive operations.
Javani said Iran had never initiated a war and that its actions to date had been defensive, but, "from now on, every action we take, although it has a defensive nature, must take on an offensive form."
Javani said a number of appointments and directives issued by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei last week reflected a broader effort to "reorganize, modernize and make more effective" Iran's defense doctrine in light of recent developments and the experience of the latest war.
He said Iran's adversaries should take the new directives seriously, "learn from these decrees and their messages that our armed forces will adopt transformative approaches."
"Perhaps they should expect strategic surprises," he added.
Trump says he has no schedule and he's "not in a hurry" to end the Iran war
President Trump told Fox News' Trey Yingst on Monday that he has "no time schedule" to end the war with Iran, but that the Islamic Republic should "put up the white flag of surrender," according to Yingst.
"I'm not in a hurry," the Fox journalist quoted the president as saying.
Mr. Trump repeated his assertion to Yingst that "the midterms have nothing to do with my thinking" on resolving the war, which the U.S. and Israel launched jointly with a first wave of strikes on Iran on February 28.
Mr. Trump told Fox there was a direct backchannel between U.S. officials and members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, but he didn't elaborate on any ongoing talks, saying only that the Iranians are "good poker players, but they're dying."
Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way"
President Trump told Fox News on Monday that the U.S. would bomb Oman if the country "gets in the way" of U.S. efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the war with Iran, according to the network's Trey Yingst.
"If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the s*** out of them," Trump said, according to Yingst's recounting of his conversation with the president.
Earlier, Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters Tehran had struck an agreement with Oman regarding shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, but did not elaborate.
Iran and Oman have held talks for weeks aimed at creating a mechanism to manage the strategic waterway in the future, with both having suggested at times that fees may be imposed for ships to use the strait. No concrete plans have been formally announced.
Despite Iran's threats and attacks on ships keeping traffic through the strait at a virtual standstill, Mr. Trump has asserted repeatedly that the U.S. is in control of the waterway, and that it may "keep it."
Kushner meets with Netanyahu after talks with Hamas leaders
President Trump's son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner met Monday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after holding talks with Hamas leaders the previous day.
The meeting came two weeks after Mr. Trump said Hamas had agreed to disarm in accordance with a U.S.-backed Gaza peace deal. Netanyahu rejected the peace proposal, insisting that Hamas must be "genuinely disarmed."
Kushner's meeting with Hamas leaders took place in Egypt, with the goal of translating the plan negotiated by Mr. Trump's Board of Peace into concrete steps, a source told CBS News.
The meeting in Egypt also included discussion of the transfer of all governing responsibilities to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, ensuring Hamas has no future governing role in Gaza, facilitating Israeli withdrawals and deploying an international stabilizing force in the region, among other things, the source told CBS News.
Iran says agreement on future routes through Strait of Hormuz reached with Oman
Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that Tehran had reached an agreement with Oman on routes for ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz in the future.
Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters in Tehran "an understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route."
Baghaei did not elaborate on the route or whether any fees would be imposed on ships using it, but both Iran and Oman have previously suggested commercial vessels should enter the Strait of Hormuz using a route close to Iran's coast, and exit it using another near Omani waters.
Baghaei said both sides were working to finalize details before issuing a joint statement on the matter.
Iran considers missing pilots to be prisoners in Qatar
Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that it would consider three missing pilots to be prisoners in Qatar, despite denials by Qatari officials, until Doha offers clarity on the fate of the missing personnel.
Tehran has said the Iranians went missing while carrying out an operation against the United States' Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar on March 2, shortly after the outbreak of the war.
On Saturday, Iranian authorities alleged for the first time that the pilots had been captured in Qatar, after previously saying one pilot had been killed and three others were missing following their sortie.
"It is imperative to obtain clarification on their situation," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said during a weekly news briefing.
"Until the pilots' situation is clarified, we consider them prisoners and will spare no effort to shed light on their fate," he said.
Iran downplays significance of 60-day negotiation period ending
Iran's foreign ministry has downplayed the importance of the 60-day period of negotiations agreed to in the memorandum of understanding with the U.S., which is due to expire Monday.
During his weekly news conference, ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran would not alter its policies due to external pressure or deadlines, adding that the period designated for negotiations was not being implemented due to ongoing U.S. strikes against the country.
"What was included in the memorandum [...] is not being implemented," he said.
"We did not commence negotiations because the United States began violating the memorandum shortly after its June 18 signing," Baghaei said. "Therefore, the 60-day issue essentially has no relevance."
Iran's army chief announces $30,000 bounty for U.S. service members
Iran's army chief announced on Sunday a reward equivalent to around $30,000 for the capture or killing of U.S. military personnel.
Speaking at a ceremony in Tehran on Sunday, Major General Amir Hatami said any Iranian who captured or killed a U.S. military service member would receive the reward of around 5 billion Iranian tomans. For any Iranian woman who captures or kills an American service member, Hatami said the reward would be doubled.
Hatami also issued fresh warnings about Iran's determination to control the Strait of Hormuz, calling it a "sacred" geopolitical asset for the Islamic republic. He said Tehran would use its full capabilities to protect the waterway and described control of the strait as an important lever in bringing the war to an end.
Shipping in Strait of Hormuz continues to slow
Transit in the Strait of Hormuz slowed this weekend, according to data by tracking firm Kpler reported by Reuters.
Only five commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday and none on Sunday, according to Kpler, compared to 31 the prior weekend.
At least one ship entered using the Iranian route, and a small tanker laden with Iranian fuel oil exited, data showed.
Some ships may pass with their transponders off, meaning they may not be detectable, but transits are still a long way from the 130 ships that traversed the strait every day before the war started.
60-day memorandum of understanding period expires Monday
Monday marks 60 days since the U.S. and Iran signed a Memorandum of Understanding that called for negotiations to reach a wider deal to end the war between the two countries and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
However, that 60-day period expires Monday amid a stalemate between the two countries and a deal seemingly nowhere in sight. Over the past two months, talks between the two sides broke down, despite President Trump repeatedly saying a deal was imminent, leading to multiple flare-ups and escalations in the fighting and a constant exchange of threats.
On July 8, Mr. Trump declared that the memorandum of understanding was "over."
Jared Kushner met with Hamas leaders in Egypt to discuss Gaza peace road map
Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and negotiator on Middle East affairs, met with Hamas leaders in Egypt on Sunday to discuss the latest U.S.-backed peace deal that seeks the group's disarmament and a road map for the transfer of power to a new government, according to a source with knowledge of the meeting.
The meeting was aimed at translating the plan negotiated by Mr. Trump's international Board of Peace into concrete, verifiable steps, the source told CBS News, including maintaining the ceasefire between Israel and Gaza, beginning to transfer all governing responsibilities to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, ensuring Hamas has no future governing role in Gaza, facilitating Israeli withdrawals and deploying an international stabilizing force to the region, among other things.
The rare meeting in Egypt with Hamas' Khalil al-Hayya was also confirmed to the Associated Press by a regional official and a Hamas official, both speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to reporters.
CENTCOM chief praises USS Abraham Lincoln crew after visit
Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, praised the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln after he visited the aircraft carrier on Saturday.
In a statement shared on social media, Cooper said his time aboard the Lincoln was "awe-inspiring."
"I wish every American could see the crew in action," he said. "You would beam with absolute pride when witnessing their camaraderie, teamwork and resilience."
The Lincoln, which has about 5,000 service members, arrived in the Middle East in January and has been supporting the U.S. war against Iran. It deployed in November 2025 to the Pacific before it moved to the Middle East. It has spent a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days. U.S. military vessels are normally deployed for about six months.
In the last few weeks, reports have emerged of mental health concerns among the crew and supply issues on board.
Cooper acknowledged the concerns in his statement, but said the Lincoln has among the lowest numbers of cases related to mental health of all the U.S. Navy's 11 active aircraft carriers.
"This doesn't mean that all is perfect," he said. "Find any of the nearly 4 million Navy veterans in America today and they will likely tell you that service at sea for long periods of time isn't for everyone. It is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways."
Cooper applauded the actions of Lincoln's leadership for "stepping up and making mental health and crew resilience a leadership priority."
The USS George Washington aircraft carrier is headed to the Middle East to relieve the Lincoln.
Asked Friday if he thought the Lincoln's deployment was too long, President Trump said it was "not nearly long enough."

Australian mushroom killer appeals triple-murder conviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:36:06 UTC
16:36:06 KST

Australian mushroom killer Erin Patterson launched an appeal Wednesday against her convictions for murdering three people in a case that drew worldwide attention.
The 51-year-old was found guilty last year of murdering her husband's parents and an elderly aunt in 2023 after serving them a beef Wellington containing lethal death cap mushrooms.
Patterson was also convicted of attempting to murder her husband's uncle, a local pastor who survived after spending weeks in hospital.
She was sentenced to life imprisonment, with parole eligibility after 33 years.
Appeals before Melbourne court
Over two days, three judges at the Court of Appeal in Melbourne will hear two appeals: Patterson's bid to overturn her convictions and a prosecution appeal seeking a longer sentence.
Patterson has asked to follow the proceedings by live video link from the maximum-security Dame Phyllis Frost Centre in Melbourne.
Her lawyers argue that she suffered several "substantial miscarriage[s] of justice" because the trial judge made errors over what evidence could be presented.
They said evidence relating to Facebook messages, cell towers and posts about death cap mushroom sightings was either irrelevant or unfairly prejudicial to Patterson.
Her lawyer also argued that evidence concerning mushroom images found on a memory card at Patterson's home was wrongly excluded.
The appeal submission further alleged a "fundamental irregularity" occurred while the jury was sequestered that "fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts," without providing further details.
Patterson's solicitor also accused prosecutors of conducting an "unfair and oppressive" cross-examination during the trial.
Before considering the substance of the appeal, the judges must determine whether Patterson has grounds to challenge her convictions.
Prosecution seeks longer sentence
Prosecutors have separately appealed Patterson's sentence, arguing that the 33-year non-parole period was "manifestly inadequate."
They said the sentencing judge erred in finding there was a substantial chance Patterson would spend years in solitary confinement, arguing that this consideration "infected" his decision.
A 12-person jury found Patterson guilty in July last year of murdering her husband Simon's parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt, Heather Wilkinson, at her home in the Victorian farming village of Leongatha.
She was also found guilty of attempting to murder Heather's husband, Ian Wilkinson, a pastor who became gravely ill but eventually recovered.

23 dead as monsoon, cyclones displace thousands in Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:34:49 UTC
16:34:49 KST

Faisal Mahmud
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
At least 23 people have died and thousands displaced across the Philippines as heavy rainfall from the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis and Maymay triggered flooding and landslides, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) said in its latest report on Monday.
Widespread flooding and landslides have affected several regions, particularly in Luzon and parts of the Visayas, forcing families to evacuate to temporary shelters as rivers overflowed and roads became impassable.
Local authorities, according to the NDRRMC, have been carrying out rescue, relief and evacuation operations in coordination with national agencies and local government units.
The report said roads, bridges and agricultural areas were damaged in multiple provinces, disrupting transportation and livelihoods. Power interruptions and water supply problems were also reported in flood-hit communities.
Assessment teams are continuing to validate reports from affected areas as weather conditions fluctuate.
The agency warned that intermittent rains could persist in the coming days, and urged residents in low-lying and landslide-prone areas to remain vigilant and follow evacuation advisories.
Government relief operations are continuing as authorities work to restore access to affected communities and provide assistance to displaced families.

Man accused of arranging fatal ambush of Microsoft manager heads to murder trial in Florida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:31:33 UTC
16:31:33 KST

A man charged with arranging the fatal ambush of a Microsoft design manager is headed to trial on Monday in Florida, more than four years after the victim was repeatedly shot outside his vehicle while his two-year-old child was strapped in a car seat.
Investigators say a tyre was placed in the road in a plot to distract and kill Jared Bridegan, 33, in Jacksonville Beach in 2022. They allege it was a murder-for-hire scheme involving his ex-wife and her current husband.
The husband, Mario Fernandez Saldana, 38, is charged with first-degree murder in Duval County court. Bridegan's former wife, Shanna Gardner, 39, is also charged with murder, though her trial won't start until September.
Bridegan and Gardner were granted a divorce in 2015. But it was followed by years of acrimony over the parenting of their two children.
Police found that Gardner “hated Mr Bridegan, hated having to share custody of the children with him and wanted him dead,” Judge London Kite wrote, summarising evidence after a bond hearing in 2024.
The alleged gunman, Henry Tenon, had pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in 2023 and agreed to testify against Fernandez Saldana. But he withdrew the plea earlier this year and will get his own trial in 2027.
Authorities said Tenon, 65, was paid at least $10,000 by Gardner and Fernandez Saldana after Bridegan's death. Tenon's DNA was also on the tyre blocking Bridegan's travel.
Bridegan was attacked shortly after returning 9-year-old twins to Gardner's home, following a regular “date night” with the children, police said.
He was driving home to St Augustine with one of the two children he had with his wife, Kirsten, whom he married in 2017.
“I am so sorry that once you had found happiness and fulfilment in life, your life was taken from you,” Kirsten Bridegan wrote on social media on their anniversary in 2024. “But I am so grateful I got to be part of those short years and that we shared so much happiness before it was too late.”
Bridegan was chief technology officer at Utah-based Clean Simple Eats before working at Microsoft, according to his obituary.

Modernism on the Watch: Preserving the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

In the heart of Ahmedabad's Navrangpura district in India sits the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium. More than just a cricket ground, the stadium stands as one of India's earliest experiments in modernist public architecture. Built in the decades following the country's independence, the structure has not only become an engineering landmark, but also a major public space within Ahmedabad's urban fabric. Despite the building's architectural and historical significance, as well as its deep involvement in daily community life, it has suffered significant physical degradation as a result of decades of poor maintenance and lack of funding. That fragility is precisely why it has drawn international attention. In 2020, the World Monuments Fund (WMF) placed the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium on its World Monuments Watch, a global list highlighting cultural heritage sites facing urgent preservation challenges.
To understand this project better, it helps to look at India during the early years after independence in 1947. Under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, the nation set out to modernize rapidly by industrializing its cities and founding new academic and civic institutions. Part of this process was also searching for an architectural language that could express a forward-looking identity distinct from its colonial past. That is why Nehru's government invited internationally renowned architects, including Le Corbusier, to help build entirely new cities and institutions, most famously the city of Chandigarh.

Two Ukrainian children attacked in Poland over speaking Ukrainian – consulate
Unknown

Two Ukrainian children attacked in Poland over speaking Ukrainian – consulate
According to Ukrinform, the consulate announced this on Facebook.
"Unfortunately, we once again have to report an extremely unacceptable incident that occurred on August 14 this year involving minor children in a park near the railway station in Bydgoszcz. Two Ukrainian minors – a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother – were subjected to aggression by adults simply because they were speaking Ukrainian to each other," the statement said.
According to the consulate, a man and a woman accompanied by a small dog not only used obscene language and made threats based on national intolerance, but also resorted to physical violence. They twisted one of the children's arms, broke a toy drone and threw the pieces at the boy, causing scratches.
Ukraine's Consulate General in Gdansk responded promptly and is keeping the case under special supervision. Consular officials remain in constant contact with the children's mother and have provided her with all necessary consular and legal assistance.
"A report of the attack has been filed, and the police are currently searching for the perpetrators," the consulate said, adding that the children are not currently in danger physically, although they have suffered severe emotional distress.
"If you witnessed this incident, which occurred in the park near the railway station, or have any information about the individuals who committed it, we strongly urge you to contact the police immediately. Your testimony is extremely important to ensure that the perpetrators are identified and brought to justice," the diplomats said.
The consulate condemned the attack as another manifestation of xenophobia.
"We strongly condemn any manifestations of xenophobia. Combating intolerance and ensuring the safety of Ukrainians will be among the key issues at a meeting planned in the coming days at the Consulate with the leadership of the Pomeranian Voivodeship, city mayors and police commanders. We will not leave this case without an appropriate legal response," the diplomats said.
On August 9, demonstrations were held in 22 Polish cities under the slogan "Don't Be Indifferent" to protest growing violence targeting Ukrainians and members of other minorities.
