2026-08-18
05:17:44 UTC
14:17:44 KST

Why Meduza’s map of the front line in Ukraine doesn’t look like DeepState’s or ISW’s, plus answers to dozens more questions from readers
This is the second installment of answers to Meduza readers’ questions about the Russia-Ukraine war. In the first, we collected your messages on two main topics — the two armies’ strategies and the strikes each side launches deep behind the other’s lines. This time we’ll take on three more big clusters of questions. The first covers the current situation at the front; the second, the drone war that is deciding the course of the whole conflict; the third, both sides’ losses and the unpopular mobilization decisions those losses might prompt.
Meduza has condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine from the very start, and we are committed to reporting objectively on a war we firmly oppose. Join Meduza in its mission to challenge the Kremlin’s censorship with the truth. Donate today. 
What’s happening at the front right now?
Is the Russian army advancing deeper into Ukraine? Please give a firm, clear answer. — Boris
It’s advancing — but in some places it’s retreating, too.
Am I right that the ruscists’ [Russian fascists’] cocky little “plans” to seize the Donbas by the end of the year, which looked questionable from the start, have now flat-out collapsed for good? And is there really any chance they’ll ever be realized at all, given that the front line is barely moving? — Oleg
Yes, a victorious end to Russia’s Donbas campaign this year looks unlikely, and there’s no guarantee of one over the medium term, either.
How do you verify your map? If you look at your map alongside maps from, say, DeepState or ISW [the Institute for the Study of War], the differences in territorial control are huge. What explains them? Subjectivity, or different methodologies? — Andrei
In your analyses, the situation at the front sometimes differs sharply from, say, DeepState’s. Can you explain in more detail what sources you use and what your criteria are for calling a town captured? — Daniil
I came across an excerpt from an ISW report claiming that in April Ukraine liberated 100 square kilometers [39 square miles] more territory than it lost. But on Meduza’s charts, the balance of territorial control has favored Russia the whole time you’ve been tracking it, going back to the Kursk operation. — Vovan
If you’re not sure which maps these readers mean, you can find them at this link. We draw them solely from geolocated video; roughly 100 new clips surface each week. We use geolocations produced by numerous research projects, checking each one ourselves, along with geolocations of our own.
To go by its own write-ups, the Ukrainian project DeepState prefers data from anonymous sources inside Ukraine’s military. Pro-Russian counterparts such as LostArmour draw on information from the Russian military instead. We have no such sources on either side, and no way to assess other projects’ sources for reliability or hidden motives — so we work exclusively from open data.
The front lines drawn by pro-Ukrainian and pro-Russian projects often contradict what’s visible in published videos. Sometimes that’s because clips are posted late — a lag occasionally detectable from the weather, the damage, and other details — but more often the cause is unreliable information from sources. Projects backing one side or the other needle each other over these discrepancies, often not gently at all: “Ukrainian soldiers in Kupyansk, which Gerasimov supposedly captured a year ago…” or “DeepState still holds Bakhmut…”
Even so, we don’t claim our rendering of the front line is the only correct one — every map is an approximation. Assessing objective data such as geolocations comes with its own difficulties, and those difficulties are growing. Beyond publication delays, there have been attempts at manipulation, from dropping flags from drones behind enemy lines (both sides have done this) to photos and videos in Russian sources that look suspiciously like AI-generated content. The only drone footage that can be fully trusted shows identifiable ground features or enemy personnel — and even then, the clips could be archival.
The war’s changing character also affects how we read video. In 2023–2024, spotting infantry or equipment from one army in a given location almost certainly meant that army controlled it. But as infiltration tactics and drone-based resupply have spread, those sightings no longer tell us nearly as much. That’s why “sleeves” and “pockets” have started appearing on our maps — areas where one side holds on to territory behind enemy lines.
The geolocations of these videos — and what they show — only make sense if both armies are increasingly willing to operate deep behind each other’s lines. In Kostyantynivka, for example, where Russian troops have long moved through nearly the entire city, Ukrainian positions held on at least until early August, as numerous videos of Russian drone strikes show. The same was true farther south in Toretsk in 2025, where Ukrainian positions sat deep behind Russian lines for months. Some may have been, and may still be, completely surrounded, resupplied only by drones or ground-based remote-controlled vehicles. But because front-line formations on both sides are so thin, it’s often possible to slip out of such an encirclement relatively safely.
Infiltration depth during offensives has also grown. A year ago, assault troops might unexpectedly turn up a couple of kilometers beyond the previous front line; now those distances reach 10–15 kilometers (6–9 miles), because so little infantry remains on either side’s front-line positions. These aren’t isolated cases — the phenomenon has spread, at least on the Russian side, to many sections of the front.
Assessing these geolocations, and especially plotting them on maps, isn’t simple. Analysts biased toward one side or the other are tempted to explain away enemy assault troops turning up behind their own lines as suicide fighters sent in for show. But in most cases, the goal of these infiltrations isn’t to manipulate public opinion — it’s to shake loose the enemy’s defenses, for instance by knocking out drone operators behind the lines. When infiltrations in a given area keep recurring in growing numbers, that can fairly be called an attempt to establish control.
We believe our rendering generally captures both the dynamics and the nature of the fighting: the more “sleeves” there are, the more unstable the situation in a given area.
As for the ratio of “control zones,” that’s not the most useful metric. Taken at face value, it would rank August 2024 as one of Ukraine’s most successful months — when Ukrainian troops seized vast territory in the Kursk region even as they kept losing ground in the southern Donbas at an accelerating pace. By the same logic, the Russian army’s record stretch would be late February and early March 2022. The metric does convey something — it reflects the slowdown in the Russian advance in 2026, for instance — but the details are more complicated. Right now, Ukrainian gains at the junction of the Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Donetsk regions are canceling out the Russian advance in the Donbas. But Russian advances still seem to carry greater “value” in terms of their effect on the strategic situation.
The gap in the absolute area each side is credited with capturing comes down to two things: the differing information sources noted above, and DeepState’s use of a huge “gray zone,” behind which actual Russian territorial gains are often hidden. We don’t count the “gray zone” — though it certainly exists, and its depth varies considerably from one part of the front to another.
Why don’t you report on the real situation in Kostyantynivka? It’s already lost to Ukraine. Your map is nonsense — those long “sleeves” simply can’t run that deep into Russian positions. Anyone with common sense who asks “how is that even supplied?” or “how are they holding the flanks?” can see plainly that you’re lying. — Pyotr
Numerous videos show positions in Kostyantynivka being supplied by drones and unmanned ground vehicles. Ukrainian forces did fail to hold the flanks, but that didn’t stop them from maintaining a presence in the city and even bringing reinforcements into the northern outskirts and the city center as late as the end of July. Ukrainian commanders used the same tactic in Pokrovsk over the winter to keep Russian forces from setting up drone operator positions and the rest of what they need to spot and hit targets before advancing on Dobropillia.
The most recent videos of Ukrainian positions and Russian strikes inside Kostyantynivka appeared on August 11 (northern outskirts), August 10 (western part), and August 3 (eastern part). Clips like these are growing rarer. Russian assault troops have already pushed north of the city, where they were spotted and came under fire on the outskirts of Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka.
What’s happening in the city of Lyman? Who controls it? Who has the greater initiative, Russia or Ukraine? — Alexei V.
Judging by videos from recent weeks, the initiative in Lyman has shifted to Ukraine. Russian forces stormed the city in July and were spotted in every district except the western outskirts. But subsequent videos show dozens of Russian strikes on those same districts, and several recent clips reportedly show Russian troops still fighting inside the built-up area. Even so, there’s no objective confirmation that Ukrainian forces have retaken southern Lyman — one recent video shows Russian troops on the southeastern outskirts. Ukrainian forces are also still attempting counterattacks north of the city toward Zarichne, while Russian forces try to push through to the Siverskyi Donets River at various points around Lyman.
I’m very worried that once the Russian army takes the rest of the Donetsk region, it’ll start storming the city of Zaporizhzhia. Do you think this is part of their plans, and how much time do civilians still have to evacuate in relative safety? — Zaporizhzhia
Please explain why neither side is using the drained Kakhovka Reservoir to attack the other or to slip into enemy territory. — Dmitry
Russian forces are pushing toward Zaporizhzhia independent of the Donbas offensive, and the reasons are political. First, under the “spirit of Anchorage,” the Zaporizhzhia region is to be split along the line of contact as it stands when a ceasefire is signed — giving Vladimir Putin an incentive to seize as much of it as possible beforehand. Second, the Kremlin has said repeatedly that if Volodymyr Zelensky doesn’t hand over the Donbas voluntarily, “the demands could change” once it’s captured. Advancing as close as possible to the Zaporizhzhia region’s capital now would lay the groundwork for a new ultimatum.
For now, Russian forces lack the strength to break through to Zaporizhzhia. That could change if the Donbas falls.
This is where the Kakhovka Reservoir comes in — or more precisely, the offensive by Russia’s “Dnipro” group of forces, which was reinforced with airborne units moved up to the shore of the former reservoir. In the spring, Russian forces reached Richne on the Konka River, 12 kilometers (7 miles) from Zaporizhzhia’s southern outskirts. But a Ukrainian counterattack — including a push into the open flank across the former reservoir bed — drove Russian troops out of Richne along with Prymorske and most of Stepnohirsk. Ukrainian forces advanced up to 12 kilometers (7 miles) from north to south. The attack also eliminated a dangerous Russian wedge east of Stepnohirsk that threatened the Orikhiv–Zaporizhzhia road. Ukrainian assault troops are now operating south of Stepnohirsk. The upshot is that Ukraine has retaken nearly all the territory it lost in this Russian offensive, except for part of the village of Kamianske.
Ukraine’s success here may owe something to Russian troop rotations. In recent months, only one regiment of the 7th Mountain Air Assault Division has been spotted in the area — not the rest of the airborne forces that took part in the offensive. The Russian force there now consists mostly of reserve regiments, the equivalent of Ukraine’s territorial defense units.
For now, residents of Zaporizhzhia face no added danger beyond “routine” drone and missile strikes. The signs that the city risks ending up in the front-line zone would be a new offensive along the reservoir’s shore that puts Russian forces on the Konka, or the capture of Orikhiv and an advance north of it. Even short of an assault on the city itself, either move would make life difficult, at least in Zaporizhzhia’s southern districts — much as it has been in Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, where Russian forces can already strike with first-person-view (FPV) drones and artillery, sharply worsening conditions across the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk metro area.
Capturing Orikhiv is clearly part of Russian commanders’ near-term plans, though the fighting is still confined to the city’s outskirts. Alongside the “Dnipro” group of forces, units from the “Vostok” group of forces are approaching from the east — but again, these threats remain a distant prospect.
I want to understand what’s going on with Mala Tokmachka. When did the fighting for this village begin? How has it progressed? And has there really been active combat there this whole time? — Arnold from Los Angeles
We’ve already covered the full backstory of the fighting around Mala Tokmachka.
In short, the fighting in this area — the front south of Orikhiv in the Zaporizhzhia region — is smaller in scale than the meme’s fame would suggest. The meme grew out of that place name being repeated for months on end in pro-Russian battlefield reports — and out of the fact that the name is hard to forget.
In recent days, the situation for Ukrainian forces around Mala Tokmachka has sharply worsened. Russian troops from the “Vostok” grouping are gradually closing in on Orikhiv from the east, and — likely as a result — Russian units have broken through to the city’s outskirts from the south via Novodanylivka, reaching a stretch of the Mala Tokmachka–Orikhiv highway. It’s not yet clear whether they’ve established a foothold there, but recent videos show Russian assault troops still fighting within Orikhiv’s city limits, on the outskirts. It’s worth remembering that similar crises in Ukraine’s defense have occurred before without leading to Russian success — which is partly how the meme about “eternal battles for a strategic village” got started.
Can you tell us about the Ukrainian offensive over the past six months and the influence of drones on it? — Kancellor
Both armies are developing new combined-arms tactics centered on heavy drone use.
The principles are the same on both sides: drones and artillery locate and destroy the enemy’s drone operator positions, a process that takes several weeks. Once enemy fire has been weakened, assault groups move in — and lately, these groups have also been used directly in combat against drone operators.
The drawbacks are shared too: offensives unfold slowly, broken into stages that each require separate preparation.
As for Ukraine’s own offensive operations, they have lately been concentrated almost entirely in the Zaporizhzhia region, ever since the winter counteroffensive at Kupyansk ended. Russian forces are attacking at Kupyansk again. We described the successful Ukrainian attacks against the Russian “Dnipro” grouping south of Zaporizhzhia above. At the junction of the Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Donetsk regions, a larger Ukrainian offensive has been underway for several months, with forces roughly the size of an army corps that commanders pulled in from near Dobropillia and the Sumy region. The operation amounts to repeated strikes against the flank of the Russian “Vostok” grouping where it meets the “Tsentr” grouping. The latter is mainly advancing on Dobropillia.
Ukrainian forces have pushed 10–15 kilometers (6–9 miles) into Russian defenses in several areas. Russian commanders have shored up that flank, moving in forces from near Dobropillia and from the western flank of the Kramatorsk offensive. In recent days, Ukrainian forces have fought their way to the intersection of the Donetsk–Zaporizhzhia highway and the road to Velyka Novosilka, a town vital to Russian rear-area logistics and to supplying the “Vostok” grouping.
Ukrainian commanders’ next moves are unclear: they could push toward Velyka Novosilka to get behind the “Vostok” group of forces, or along the Zaporizhzhia-Donetsk road to get behind the Russian 90th Tank Division from the “Tsentr” grouping. The “Vostok” grouping’s Telegram channel recently published dozens of videos showing Russian assault troops in villages Ukraine had previously liberated, and it’s still unclear who actually controls that territory.
So far, the offensive has partially achieved two goals — pulling some Russian forces away from the Kramatorsk sector, and slowing, though not stopping, the “Vostok” grouping’s advance west toward Orikhiv.
You keep writing that it will take the Russian army a long time to capture territory if you go by its current rate of advance. But once the main fortresses fall, shouldn’t there be open country to maneuver in, without prepared fortifications? — Ivan
Suppose Russian forces take Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Suppose the war doesn’t end there. Where would Ukraine’s next defensive line be, and what are the prospects for defending it? — Olya
The military significance of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk — not their political significance — is overstated. The two cities do serve as the “last fortresses” on Russia’s path deeper into Ukraine. That’s not because they’re weak “fortresses,” but because of their geography: to their north and northeast lie woodland and the Siverskyi Donets River, an obstacle that stopped Russian forces cold when they tried to storm the two cities from the north in 2022. In effect, the cities defend themselves — and with them, Ukraine’s sovereignty over the Donbas.
Zelensky, explaining his reluctance to surrender the Donbas, has said Russian forces could push north from Kramatorsk and Sloviansk into the Kharkiv region by crossing the Siverskyi Donets — though Russia already holds better positions for attacking that region.
There have also been suggestions that Russian forces could advance on the city of Dnipro from Kramatorsk. But here too, better routes exist, from the Zaporizhzhia region and Pokrovsk — so Russian commanders clearly have no such plans for now.
Ukraine has been building fortifications in the west and north of the Donetsk region for several months now. If the Ukrainian army avoids defeat at Kramatorsk, the prospects for defending new lines will be at least as good as they were for the line west of Pokrovsk, a city Russian forces captured more than six months ago. The catch is that if the Donetsk region falls entirely, Russian commanders would be free to redeploy troops elsewhere along the front — which is exactly why there’s a real military logic for Ukraine in tying those forces down in front of well-defended “fortresses.”
What is the “front” in this war? In videos I see small groups of soldiers constantly driving somewhere, moving somewhere else, hiding somewhere. Is the front line a clear line, or is it a gray [combat] zone about 50 kilometers [31 miles] wide? — Vitaliy
Why wouldn’t throwing in huge numbers of infantry (in line with current tactics, of course — infiltration in tiny groups) break the front open? Say 10,000 North Koreans go out in pairs, spaced 100 meters [330 feet] apart along a 50-kilometer [31-mile] stretch of front, every half hour. Would the drone guys really spot and kill every last one of them? — Senya
We’re used to defining the “kill zone” as a strip that no one can cross because they’ll inevitably be killed by a drone. But the front does move, however slowly, which means the kill zone does get crossed sometimes. How is that achieved, and what differences are there between current Russian and Ukrainian tactics? — Alexander
I’d like a general, high-level picture of what the war looks like for most of the people fighting it. We see hyped-up drone footage. Footage of actual small-arms combat is very rare. So what does daily life look like for these hundreds of thousands of people? Say, roughly, 20% are in the rear, 50% are in spots where not much happens, 20% go on assaults, and 10% supply all of them. In general, what does an average day at war look like? What does a typical battle look like? — Vladislav
Drone videos get published so often not just because the entire war runs on drone strikes, but because this footage is easy to obtain. The “kill zone” isn’t actually impenetrable to everything living, and the gray zone doesn’t run 50 kilometers (31 miles) deep.
Because drones saturate the front line and the ground just behind it — up to 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the line of contact — concentrating troops really is impossible. That’s not so much because everyone “will inevitably be killed”: those who don’t need to move constantly have learned to hide, though equipment is harder to conceal. The real problem is that large forces can’t be supplied, since the units handling resupply have to move across open ground. So troops are spread out in depth as much as possible. Most troops are behind the lines or tied up in supply work, and they take heavy losses.
Almost no large strongpoints remain, given the danger from glide bombs — Ukraine’s air force uses these too, though on a smaller scale than Russia’s. The best way to hide is to disperse, so enemy reconnaissance doesn’t judge a position worth one of these munitions.
The front line itself is very thin. A tree line or a farm might be held by no more than a handful of troops, attacked in turn by groups just as small. Drones and sensors — cameras — handle surveillance and target identification, while other drones and artillery strike the targets. Artillery’s range is limited because gun positions have to sit far behind the lines.
Units and entire formations spend weeks destroying each other’s weapons systems and surveillance equipment, all to create an opening for small groups to advance and dig in. To that end, every unit and formation fields its own assault detachments.
Most troops spend their time building positions behind the lines, maintaining supply routes, handling resupply — including on foot — and evacuation.
Offensives often manage to breach the first line of defense but never achieve a breakthrough on an operational scale. In 2025, assault detachments from two brigades of the 51st Army broke deep behind Ukrainian lines between Dobropillia and Druzhkivka, but supplying them proved impossible.
Please tell us how realistic it is, with the troops and equipment they’ve got, to storm big cities like Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. The Lysychansk–Sievierodonetsk operation was carried out with a 1-to-10 ratio of shells fired, full depots, and Korean deliveries. The situation now is different. — Ahasfer
Russian forces now storm cities, as Colonel Abdulaziz Shikhabidov put it to Putin, “through the active use of new techniques and methods of conducting combat operations.” The core approach is unchanged: drones for reconnaissance, and strike drones, aviation, and artillery to suppress the enemy’s weapons systems, followed by assault troops — for whom operating in cities is often easier than in other terrain, thanks to the abundance of places to take cover.
Artillery has grown far more accurate and now expends fewer shells per target, chiefly not because of precision-guided munitions but because it has been folded into a single loop with reconnaissance drones. But it has fewer targets available and has been pushed far back from the front, which keeps it from firing deep into enemy territory. Its role has shrunk as a result, and drones have taken over much of its work.
Over four years of war, I’ve often heard in the media about fighting in towns with the same names. Is that just a coincidence, or are there areas where the front has been “frozen” since the start of the war? — Maxim
Sometimes it’s because the front has stayed static in certain areas. But there’s another reason: identical place names are common across eastern Ukraine. In 2024–2025, for instance, Russian media reported three separate times that Russian forces had captured the village of Shevchenko, home to Ukraine’s largest, still-undeveloped lithium ore deposit. Only the third time was it actually that Shevchenko — all three villages happened to be located in roughly the same district.
There’s a front line stretching hundreds of kilometers. Along it and just behind it are villages, towns, and cities where fighting has gone on for months. I don’t really understand how life there actually works and what happens before an offensive and after these towns are taken. And if Ukrainian forces manage to retake a place, do they bring in construction equipment, and then people come back? Or how does it work? — Alexander
As Russian forces approach, Ukrainian authorities order the mandatory evacuation of children and, together with volunteer groups, try to move everyone else out too. A small number of residents, mostly elderly people, stay behind, and Russian forces then try to evacuate them. Many villages and towns are destroyed almost completely during the fighting and can’t be rebuilt — yet people often remain in them.
All the experts say that with drones everywhere, classic offensives are impossible. Why don’t Russia or Ukraine attack through the forests of Bryansk or Chernihiv, where drones would have a much harder time? — Jeff Albertson
Why isn’t there fighting in the Bryansk and Chernihiv regions? There aren’t any fortifications there on either side, so wouldn’t it be easier for both sides to advance? — Alexei
Fighting in forests poses the greatest difficulties either army faces in this war. The chief problems are supplying one’s own troops, locating the enemy with standard reconnaissance equipment, and the ease with which wooded terrain can be mined. Large offensives, as a result, cannot be mounted in forests. Individual operations are still carried out there, however — in the forests of the Sumy region, for example.
As for the northern border regions specifically, neither side has enough spare forces to extend the front line in that direction.
How likely is it that Ukraine could mount a counteroffensive on the scale of the 2022 operation in the 2026–2027 campaign? — Oliver
By fall 2022, Ukrainian forces had completed their first waves of mobilization and deployment and held a significant numerical advantage — one Russian forces could offset only by launching their own mobilization and letting the Russian mercenary group Wagner recruit tens of thousands of convicts as assault troops.
The situation now is fundamentally different: there’s no numerical advantage. Ukrainian forces are fighting with even fewer formations than the Russian military fields, and many of those formations suffer from a chronic shortage of personnel and equipment.
How will the situation at the front change after the resignation of Ukrainian Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and the appointment of Mykhailo Drapatyi? It’s hard to say for now, but many Ukrainians didn’t take Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov’s resignation well. I don’t know if Zelensky is making the right decisions on this. — Alexei
We’ve written about this in detail.
In short, Drapatyi faces a choice: stick with his predecessor’s methods, or push through a sweeping reform that changes tactics and operational practice at the front. Whichever path he takes, he’ll face major political and military problems.
It appears Drapatyi has decided — as had been discussed in former Defense Minister Fedorov’s circle — to dismantle Syrskyi’s main instrument: assault regiments that had swelled to the size of divisions and served as “fire brigades.” The military has begun transferring “surplus” personnel from some regiments to regular brigades, and there’s also talk of moving out the entire roster of brigades judged unfit for combat.
The reform has advantages: it unifies and simplifies command, and it eases tensions within units that resented what they saw as an unfair distribution of resources to the assault regiments. It also has drawbacks. Restructuring the system in the middle of a Russian offensive and cutting the number of formations could cause trouble at the front.
Who’s winning the drone war?
Why is the Russian military falling so far behind in the number and quality of drones? — Andrei
There’s no major gap between Russian and Ukrainian forces in the number of drones, whether FPV, reconnaissance, or long-range — at times Russia has even led, for example when it was first to deploy fiber-optic drones. But Russian forces have fallen significantly behind in the number and quality of interceptor drones capable of countering long-range strike drones, and are now trying to catch up.
The two sides copy each other’s solutions. Ukrainian manufacturers and the military quickly adopted fiber-optic drones; Russia, in turn, has copied many of Ukraine’s organizational moves in recent months, including the creation of a separate drone branch of the armed forces. Both armies are working to introduce and improve machine-vision drones, and Russian forces are also developing combined-arms tactics built around drones at the front — again, largely mirroring Ukraine’s approach.
Innovation in Russia appears to have stalled in recent months, as development has gradually been centralized under state control. Coordination between drone operators and other units at the front has also sharply worsened since the shutdown of smuggled Starlink terminals, which Russian forces had relied on heavily.
The impression that Russia is falling behind comes from the past year’s increase in Ukrainian strikes on targets deep inside Russia. Ukraine, meanwhile, has been living under constant drone attack for far longer.
In recent months, Russia has stopped trying to attack with piston-engine drones like the “Geran-2.” That’s probably because Ukraine’s air defenses work. Why can’t Russia protect itself the same way from attacks by piston-engine FP-1 and FP-2 drones? What would it take to do that? — “NATO instructor”
Russia continues to use piston-engine drones even as it rapidly ramps up production of jet-powered ones. It deploys the “Geran-2” wherever Ukraine lacks dense air defense, while relying more often on jet-powered “Geran-3Ts” and “Geran-4” drones against the Kyiv and Odesa areas.
On the whole, Russia has fallen behind in developing specialized counter-drone defenses — both interceptors and the reconnaissance and control systems behind them.
If reconnaissance drones are flying everywhere and both sides know where everyone is, why don’t they use heavy weapons to hit the spots where drone operators are hiding? Why aren’t they trying to kill [Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert Brovdi] Madyar? — Robert
That’s exactly what Russian and Ukrainian forces are doing — drone operator positions rank among the priority targets. But identifying them is extremely difficult. Operators site their control antennas away from where they sit, avoid anything that could give away their position, and work from basements where they can. Strikes on their positions still happen regularly, though Madyar’s own location is likely even harder to pin down.
I have more of a technical question about drone attacks. Today, massive drone attacks on large cities often happen without anyone warning residents. Please explain why this is. It’s hard to imagine that with modern technology, radar and satellites can’t at least detect large groups of drones. — Natalya
Low-flying drones really are hard to detect — American troops who have themselves come under attack from Iranian “Shahed” drones say the same thing. Tracking drones along their entire flight path is even harder: that takes a dense network of sensors — not just radars — or airborne radars, or both. And the quality of Russia’s air defense information system, which is supposed to pull together data on every target, leaves a great deal to be desired. The Russian Defense Ministry has promised to build a new system by November.
What real evidence is there that fully autonomous AI drones are being used widely in this war? Not cases with autolock-on (which the operator still approves), or even the ability to fly toward a target autonomously for a few seconds, but genuinely fully autonomous flight and attack on a target? — Andrei
Fully autonomous drones aren’t in widespread use yet, but the drones you describe, with autolock-on and self-guidance onto a target, are already common on both sides.
Experiments are certainly underway. But according to limited open-source information from drone manufacturers and operators, key questions remain unresolved — how to distinguish military from civilian targets, and how reliably drones can find camouflaged ones — and experienced human operators still perform these tasks better. Manufacturers, moreover, find it more cost-effective when mass-producing drones to rely on ready-made commercial solutions, like cameras with built-in autolock and object tracking.
So one of the main problems with drones — guidance difficulties at low altitude caused by lost communication — is being solved. Another — the need to assign a dedicated operator to every remotely piloted drone — is not.
I keep reading news headlines like “300 drones were headed for Moscow today” or “240 drones were shot down overnight in region N.” And this happens two or three times a week. If the headlines are accurate, that means thousands of drones are being produced a month. I don’t understand how you run production like that in the middle of a war, how much money and time goes into producing one drone, how such a large number of drones is transported to their launch sites, and whether this investment “pays off” in terms of the cost-to-damage ratio. — Spider-Man
On the exact number of drones, the authorities can’t be trusted. Most likely, they don’t know themselves how many drones were in each wave, and the summary reports they hand to the media, drawn from air defense information systems, are often quite inaccurate. Authorities also tamper with the numbers, and sometimes stop publishing them altogether — signs of manipulation show up not just in Russia and Ukraine but also, for example, in the public communications of Persian Gulf states.
Still, there’s no doubt both Russia and Ukraine use hundreds of drones in each “salvo.” Their main advantage is low cost — both of producing each individual unit and of organizing production at scale. They rely on standard commercial electronics, parts made from simple composites and 3D-printed components, and engines that are almost all foreign, usually mass-produced Chinese piston and turbojet motors. Drones are often delivered to their launch sites by civilian trucks.
As for “payoff,” it depends on which metric you use. Drones certainly destroy military and civilian property worth far more than the drones themselves cost, and more than was spent building the production capacity behind them. Could those resources have been spent differently for a greater military effect? Possibly.
Why doesn’t either side try to use light trainer aircraft against drones? The L-39, Yak-130, or Yak-152 aren’t built for combat, but they could carry machine guns, they have enough range, and are very maneuverable, especially compared to Russian “Shahed” drones or Ukrainian FP drones. — Volodya Shchepotkin
Ukraine uses aircraft like these for exactly that purpose — both the Yak-52 and the L-39. Negotiations are underway to purchase a large batch of L-39s upgraded specifically to counter drones, and Russia may be using the L-39 as well. Aviation, including helicopters, is a necessary element of counter-drone defense — only aircraft are mobile enough to cover a large area.
Talking to various people, I keep hearing the same idea: that Ukraine’s attack drones are launched from Russian (or EU) territory. These people don’t know each other, so apparently this view is spreading somewhere on the “other” side. Is there any evidence for this claim, and what can be said against it? — Alexandra
This is a well-known urban legend, likely spawned by Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) “Spiderweb” operation, in which small FPV drones were smuggled by truck across Russian territory to military airfields and used to strike long-range bombers. Relatively large drones — some of which, early in the war, were built on light-aircraft airframes — are far harder to move overland than by air. There’s no evidence these drones have ever been launched from Russia or any neighboring country other than Ukraine, though Russia’s Foreign Ministry, of course, is happy to keep the legend alive.
Every night, Russian monitoring channels that draw on air defense unit reports show the same picture: Ukrainian drones appear over the Bryansk and Belgorod regions, over the Donbas, Crimea, the Sea of Azov, and the Black Sea, then punch deep into the country and fly their planned routes to their targets.
I live in the Moscow region, not far from an airport. From spring 2025 on, drone attacks meant everything got jammed for two to four days: mobile service, internet, even television. Since June 2026, drones are shot down almost every day, and yet everything keeps working. Why did they stop blocking communications? Has something changed in how the drones are built? Or was there never much military or technical sense to the blocking in the first place? — Lilya
Does shutting off mobile internet (introducing whitelists) help fight drones? Or are they guided by GPS and Starlink, so whitelists don’t get in their way at all? — Igor
Authorities took up blocking mobile communications after the “Spiderweb” operation too, since Ukrainian FPV drones were indeed controlled via GSM modems at the time. But the long-range drones that Ukraine’s military and the SBU use to strike Russia daily mostly don’t rely on mobile communications — so the shutdowns are useless against them.
Starlink isn’t used for strikes either, since it doesn’t work in Russia — except in the coastal zone of the Krasnodar region, where Ukraine has managed to build mesh networks centered on a satellite communications terminal. But Kyiv is trying to persuade Elon Musk to switch on Starlink coverage over Russia for Ukrainian military devices, which would let drones strike mobile military targets such as “Iskander” ballistic missile launchers, fighter jets, and bombers sitting on airfields.
The main control channel for long-range drones is an inertial system that receives corrections from a satellite navigation receiver.
How does electronic warfare equipment work, and how does it affect drones? There are videos of drones veering off course because of electronic warfare and crashing into houses, but a drone’s flight is powered by its engine. The engine can’t just stall because of electronic warfare. So why do drones fall? — Yegor
The control system for long-range drones periodically receives GPS corrections to fix errors in its inertial navigation. Systems that feed drones a false GPS signal — “spoofing” — are widespread in both Russia and Ukraine, and anyone who uses digital maps has probably run into one. If that signal is substituted at the moment it’s received, the drone’s onboard computer recalculates its route to the target from the false location. Sometimes that leads to incidents in which civilians are killed.
What speed and altitude do drones fly at? How do they maneuver? I used to think they flew in from the west. But in Chekhov this week, a drone hit the eastern (!) side of an apartment building. A drone headed toward a Wildberries warehouse in Yekaterinburg on July 25 seemed to be coming from the southeast. So can drones take a detour mid-flight? I thought that if you live on the east side of a building, there’s almost no risk. — Max
Drones can indeed maneuver, following waypoints programmed into their flight path, with routes plotted to avoid detected air defense systems and mobile anti-drone gun teams.
You publish a lot of photos of military equipment covered by metal anti-drone nets, some of them pretty inventive. 1) How effective are they? 2) Could the same kind of nets be used to protect buildings (refineries, warehouses, etc.)? — James
Metal nets make strikes on equipment more expensive, since hitting a single target now takes more drones. There have been attempts to cover individual refinery units the same way, but no data showing it helped. Hiding a huge object under metal netting is obviously neither as simple nor as cheap as covering a tank, and drones attacking plants and warehouses carry tens of kilograms of explosives — far more than the few kilograms carried by the FPV drones that hunt armored vehicles.
Why not simply use all of Ukraine’s drone production capacity to destroy military targets at the front line, specifically to destroy military equipment? — Alexei
How would the situation in the war change if Ukraine used its long-range drones for closer targets tied to Russian logistics? It seems like strikes on oil refineries and Wildberries warehouses work more as psyops, while Russian forces keep advancing. Or are long-range drones simply not as effective in front-line conditions? — Nikodim
Entirely different drones are used for strikes on front-line targets. They’re smaller and much cheaper, but they carry the camera needed to hit moving targets. For strikes on logistics — also moving targets, but dozens of kilometers back from the front — intermediate variants are being developed: drones built to strike targets deeper behind the lines. These are the drones hunting fuel trucks on the highway from the Rostov region to Crimea, or trucks and electric locomotives inside Ukraine. Russia does sometimes use “Geran” drones fitted with a video camera controlled over mesh networks for strikes closer to the front.
Long-range drones can also be used against military warehouses, and these strikes happen regularly. But unlike the online retailer Wildberries, the military long ago overhauled its logistics system in the front-line zone: instead of the huge, often open storage sites typical of 2022, a network of small, well-camouflaged warehouses now covers the area.
What losses are the two sides taking, and could this lead to another mobilization in Russia?
Ukrainian politicians have recently talked a lot about Russia preparing a new wave of forced mobilization, and naturally, you’ve asked us many questions about this scenario. This isn’t the first time — similar warnings after 2022 didn’t pan out — which makes it tempting to file this discussion under Kyiv’s psychological operations too. Still, the possibility is worth taking seriously, so we’ve laid out some brief context before answering your questions.
Over the past three years, the Kremlin has clearly been satisfied with how the regions have handled their contract-recruitment quotas. Russian authorities launched that campaign at full capacity in mid-2023, assigning each governor a quota, and those targets have barely changed since, even as Russian losses mounted. Russian forces could form entire new armies and corps from scratch in 2023 and 2024, but that process has all but stopped. Meanwhile, regions are paying more and more to attract new contract soldiers — regional “signing bonuses” keep climbing, even though the government has raised the federal bonus only once, back in 2024.
So it’s fair to say the conditions for replenishing the army with contract soldiers and volunteers have worsened, yielding smaller returns than three years ago. Yet the Kremlin has refused to shift to compulsory measures this entire time — Putin apparently judges the social and economic risks of a new mobilization wave too high relative to the potential benefits.
Could that calculation change? Two kinds of developments could push it in that direction.
A decline in the number of contract soldiers even as payments rise, and/or a rise in losses to a level where recruitment no longer offsets attrition
Ukraine reports that’s exactly what’s happening now. Kyiv’s “victory plan” in part assumes that Ukrainian forces will kill 30,000 or more Russian troops a month, matching the number Russia recruits over the same period, and that level, it’s claimed, was already reached in late 2025. But everything we know about Russian losses gives reason to doubt those estimates. We’ll soon update our own tally and report, with facts, what Russian losses in killed and missing have actually been.
Even if attrition exceeds the number of new recruits, the problem could clearly be addressed without compulsory mobilization — for example, by raising regional quotas. Right now, the Kremlin requires regions to supply 0.3% of their population to the army each year. Budget reporting from roughly 40 regions shows the quota barely varies from region to region and hasn’t changed over time. Governors would obviously find it harder to meet a raised target set in Moscow, but a new wave of mobilization would be harder still.
A Putin decision to speed up the offensive and/or reinforce the army
The problems with that decision have long been clear.
Contract-soldier recruitment quotas remain at their current level because that’s the most people the army can “absorb,” that is, train and equip. Individual soldiers don’t fight alone; units do, and units need officers, both combat and staff. Formations such as brigades, divisions, and armies need support elements, too: air defense, electronic warfare, logistics, artillery, and now thousands-strong drone-operator units.
The Kremlin has already seen what forced mobilization does — it caused public discontent and drove people to flee the country, so the social and political risks are real. There’s a financial dimension too. For 300,000 newly mobilized troops, say, the federal budget alone would have to pay more than a trillion rubles in the first year, by a conservative estimate — bonuses, salaries, additional payments, and death and injury compensation.
Still, the Defense Ministry is probably unhappy with the recruits it’s currently getting — it’s hard to build high-tech units for the “army of the future” out of people who are risking their lives for money because they’re desperate. That discontent may run deep enough that the Defense Ministry could persuade the Kremlin to recruit an entirely different pool of people by force.
Over the past year, Russian forces have tried to recruit several tens of thousands of drone operators among students and other young people, offering a guaranteed short-term contract with no right of transfer to other branches of service. Students apparently didn’t trust the army, though, and the campaign failed.
The Defense Ministry made a similar attempt to staff the mobile gun teams that shoot down drones away from the front, this time driven by cost rather than skill: recruiters tried to draw fighters from the reserve pool, people who receive small payments from the army for showing up to short annual training sessions. There’s been no word of success there either.
It’s conceivable the Kremlin will eventually decide forced mobilization can solve the recruit-quality problem. For now, though, that remains purely speculative.
And now, your questions:
When people discuss the possibility of a new mobilization wave in Russia, they say it wouldn’t do much good at the front. But couldn’t Russian forces use an additional 350,000–500,000 mobilized troops to extend the line of contact along the entire Russia–Ukraine border, thereby stretching Ukraine’s defenses (especially given the shortage of Ukrainian personnel) and speeding up the advance in the Donbas and other sections of the front? Wouldn’t this extension of the line of contact fundamentally change the situation at the front? — Max from Novosibirsk
The problem is the same one: it’s not individual soldiers who fight, but units and formations, and those need commanders experienced in modern warfare, vehicles, and up-to-date weapons — all of which costs a great deal of money.
Creating 10–20 new combined-arms armies would certainly transform the situation at the front. That change wouldn’t even require extending the active front line — on many current sectors, Russian commanders are already clearly short of forces.
I’ve noticed that when bodies of the dead are exchanged between Russia and Ukraine, the numbers are always lopsided in Russia’s favor — roughly speaking, Moscow hands Kyiv 500 bodies of Ukrainian soldiers and gets 30 back in return. Meanwhile, analysts say Russia’s losses in this war are larger than Ukraine’s. So how can this discrepancy be explained? — Denis
A familiar question, and a familiar answer: over the past three years, the tactical-level battlefield has generally stayed in Russian hands. That’s not very visible on the map, but “on the ground” it plays out exactly that way — Russian burial teams can collect both their own and enemy dead, while Ukrainian teams often can’t. The last time Ukraine handed over more bodies than it received was in late summer 2023, when Ukrainian forces were still conducting their major counteroffensive. The Russian offensive that continues to this day began on October 7, 2023.
In the war’s early years, analysts liked to survey what was left at Russia’s equipment depots, using satellite imagery to track how fast old Soviet hardware was being pulled out (and, in turn, restored and put back into use). Various forecasts were made about how many years or months this equipment would last at the then-current pace of fighting. Is this analytical work continuing? — Vlad
That work continues, though its significance has diminished. Strictly speaking, these were never really forecasts — just a linear trend extrapolated forward. Had the Russian army kept losing tanks and infantry fighting vehicles at the rate of the war’s first two years, its armored vehicles would have run out by 2026. Commanders clearly recognized this and slowed the loss rate. Russian forces now have roughly as many tanks as they did before the war, thanks to new production and to restoring vehicles that had been damaged or mothballed at old Soviet storage sites. Current losses — the lowest of the war so far — are being offset by production. Slightly more videos of knocked-out Ukrainian tanks were published in 2026 than similar clips of Russian ones. But if Russian forces once again start using armored vehicles en masse in mechanized attacks, they’ll burn through their stocks quickly.
The same group of researchers is now counting losses of military trucks, a metric far more relevant given Ukraine’s campaign of strikes well behind the front lines.
On July 1, the Center for Strategic and International Studies published a review saying the two sides’ losses have already reached two million people. And while the Russian loss figures are at least plausible (450,000 killed plus a million wounded), the Ukrainian ones (150,000 plus 400,000) are questionable. P.S.: as of today, the [OSINT loss database for Ukrainian forces] UAlosses already lists 100,000 killed and just as many missing. Does CSIS really not know about this resource, or does it not trust it? And why isn’t it cited in any analysis? — Vovan
We analyzed this report in detail, and we agree with your critical assessment.
Everyone’s talking about possible mobilization in Russia (I’m there right now), but at the same time various sources, including Meduza, say that the way modern war works, most of the troops are far from the line of contact, to avoid drone strikes. If they’ve already got more than 700,000 troops there, why do they need more people when they’ll all be far from the front line anyway? — Sebastian Pereiro
Again: it’s units that fight, not individual soldiers. Those units are now spread out in depth, but they certainly don’t have a surplus of personnel — and mobilized troops would also be needed, among other things, to stand up new formations.
The only realistic scenario, in my view, is the physical exhaustion of Ukraine’s army: there’s no way to run a new mobilization there, and even after the mass exodus, the share of able-bodied people left is bigger than any plausible rate of permanent losses. What are your forecasts and scenarios for how this could develop? What might the front line look like in the event of mobilization in Russia? — Diogenes
We’ve assessed Ukraine’s mobilization capacity in a separate piece.
In short, Ukraine’s capacity to keep mobilizing will remain intact for a long time — its problems there aren’t caused by a shortage of eligible people.
As fantastical as this may sound, what would happen to the front if Russia declared martial law, closed its borders, mobilized one or two million men into “assault” units, sent the remaining men, women, children, and so on to work at defense industry plants, introduced food rationing, and used Russia’s National Guard, Rosgvardia (or something new), as enforcers… and made much greater use of North Korea? If something like that happened, how would it affect the front? — Ilon
There are serious doubts about the Russian authorities’ ability to organize and pay for all that. The Kremlin appears to sense this too, which is likely why it isn’t trying to mobilize two million people.
Is it true that defending is much easier than attacking? If Russia stopped advancing and dug in, would that significantly reduce Russian casualties? Would it make a Ukrainian offensive impossible? What I’m getting at is whether “just standing still and defending” is a good option for Russia, or whether it has no choice but to either advance or retreat. — Ivan
The Russian army has to carry out tasks consistent with the war’s political goals, which Putin sets, and those tasks are unmistakably offensive. Set the Kremlin’s goals aside, and the answer is that Russia should stop the war immediately and stop taking losses altogether.
We’re all wondering whether there’ll be mobilization after the elections, and if so, how they’d do it. Will it be covert (reservists, convicts), or like the first time? Should conscripts be worried, and how many of them are being sent to the front right now? — Roman
We largely answered the first part of this question at the start of this section. As for conscripts, they do take part in the war, but only after signing a contract — a fairly common practice. Sending conscripts to the front has been taboo for Putin since the start of his rule, though he’s never written it into law. Exceptions happen: the soldiers killed or taken prisoner in the Kursk region during the first days of Ukraine’s incursion were clearly not soldiers anyone had planned to send to war — the war simply came to them.
Why don’t tallies of permanent losses ever count deserters? They’re permanent losses too, effectively. — Alexander
For the Russian army, desertion isn’t as significant a problem, or as large a share of losses, as it is for Ukraine’s. Russian authorities had opened just over a thousand desertion cases and 26,000 cases of refusing service as of mid-2025 — there’s no more recent data. During that period, about a thousand such cases a month came before Russian courts, compared to roughly 15,000–20,000 in Ukrainian courts. That gap probably has to do with how recruitment works: Russian contract soldiers want out not during training, but once they’re already at the front, where escape is far harder. Most who want to leave simply fail to return from leave, and the army sends the majority of them back to the front without even opening a criminal case.

Burnham is choosing jobs over climate security. That’s a big risk | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

When the siren sounded on Friday night, my first thought was fire.
Weeks of unrelenting sun in the normally soggy Peak District, where I was visiting my mum, have bleached green valleys a dangerously dry, crispy blond. One of her neighbours had earlier pointed out an ominous cloud of smoke on the horizon, coming from one of the wildfires raging all summer on the moor. When that harsh, discordant shriek blared from every mobile phone in the house, I was half-braced for an evacuation order, not what turned out to be a faintly melodramatic warning to the nation to lay off the barbecues. A false alarm, of sorts, but one that felt uneasily like a wake-up call.
Scientists can warn until they’re blue in the face about the consequences of what we’re doing to the planet, but nothing beats the visceral shock of idly scrolling on your phone and seeing panicky footage of flames leaping over suburban British fences, or terrified horses being turned loose from fields where the hedges are starting to catch light. A friend just back from the south of France, somewhere far enough from the raging wildfires there to be considered safe, was spooked by ash raining from the sky as she ate lunch in the garden: it felt like the beginning of an apocalypse, she said, or the opening scenes of a disaster movie. Something has shifted even in people who were once blase about the climate crisis, and judging by last week’s sudden flurry of government activity – a Cobra meeting on fighting wildfires called after hefty pressure from the Greens, extra support for drought-stricken farmers, and finally that emergency alert lighting up everyone’s phones – Andy Burnham has clocked the dangers of not being seen to respond.
Yet there’s something jarring about a new prime minister spending the hottest summer on record talking up the prospect of new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea, or consulting on easing net zero targets for carmakers. He was rightly quick to visit people affected by a wildfire near the West Midlands town of Stourbridge, but has been noticeably slower to respond publicly to warnings from the town’s Labour MP, Cat Eccles, that this is not the time to start extracting yet more fossil fuels. So far, his is more a strategy for picking up the pieces of damage already done than for gripping the root causes.
Just how serious is Burnham about the climate crisis? It’s very early days, but a pattern is emerging that may be familiar to some in Greater Manchester, remembering the then mayor’s swift rethink of attempts to impose an unpopular clean air zone on drivers. He is not complacent about the threat to the planet – but where green policies clash with his mission to create jobs and rebuild the social fabric, Burnham and his deputy, Louise Haigh, both seem instinctively protective of the latter. This prime minister isn’t swayed by expensive fossil fuel lobbyists, but he is sensitive to unions defending the interests of oil rig workers in Aberdeen, or car manufacturers who have been warning for years that Britain’s rigid zero emission vehicle (Zev) mandate could push them into closing factories across what is left of the country’s industrial heartlands. Under the mandate, carmakers are fined if they don’t hit constantly rising targets to sell more electric cars as a percentage of total sales. If people feeling the pinch refuse to buy enough expensive new electric cars, and governments decline to subsidise them, the cheapest way of avoiding massive fines is to mothball product lines for petrol and diesel cars, to stop drivers buying too many of them.
Nobody in this government needs reminding of how a big employer closing its gates in places where jobs are scarce can rip the heart out of a community, nor how the far right feeds off that sense of hopelessness. Britain isn’t the only country considering watering down targets that few in the car industry now expect to be met. Nor, I suspect, will Burnham’s be the only government staring down the barrel of higher gas bills this autumn – caused by Donald Trump’s disastrous war on Iran – and worrying about how this new cost of living crisis might be exploited by rightwing parties blaming it on supposedly “woke” net zero policies they are desperate to revoke.
There are compelling reasons, in short, for Burnham to pitch himself as a net zero pragmatist – the word ministers keep falling back on when asked about the looming and increasingly fraught decision on drilling in the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields. (And yes, even that act of apparent climate vandalism has friends in surprising places, with the eco-entrepreneurs Dale Vince and Greg Jackson both arguing that, if we need oil and gas from somewhere, getting it from our own back yard is a cleaner option that might also help reduce the backlash against net zero.)
But if the Labour party wanted naked pragmatism, frankly it could have stuck with Keir Starmer. It looks to Andy Burnham for something more: the courage to face up to difficult questions but also the political skills to sell difficult answers, and the emotional intelligence to manage the fallout. As this unnaturally hot summer fades into what may be an equally unnaturally wet autumn, we’ll soon know whether he can actually deliver.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Half of homes in Great Britain taking longer to sell than last year amid mortgage volatility

14:00:15 KST

Half of homes in Great Britain are taking longer to sell than last year as volatile conditions in the mortgage market amid the Iran war prompt buyers to “wait and see” if they can get a better deal, according to a report.
As the Middle East conflict continues to unfold, the property platform Zoopla said homes in 180 out of 363 local authorities in England, Scotland and Wales were taking longer to sell compared with a year ago.
It said that although the national average time to sell a home had not changed – at 42 days – a widening regional gap had emerged as buyers in property hotspots raced to complete deals, while uncertainty over mortgage costs fuelled a more cautious approach elsewhere.
The report found the UK’s 10 fastest-selling markets were all in Scotland, with the lowest average time to sell at just 11 days in Falkirk. Carlisle and Barnsley in England were the fastest non-Scottish markets at 23 days each.
It said eight local authorities had an average time to sell of two months or more, led by Melton in the East Midlands, at 76 days, Westminster in London, and Teignbridge in the south-west.
Property buyers shopping for a mortgage deal have faced months of heightened volatility as the stop-start Iran war rattles financial markets – with a knock-on impact for the pricing of home loans.
The war in the Middle East led many lenders to pull deals in March, while the cost of a typical home loan soared amid fears that the conflict would reignite global inflationary pressures and force the Bank of England to raise interest rates.
The latest figures from the financial data provider Moneyfacts show the rate on an average two-year fixed residential mortgage stood at 5.61% on Monday – significantly higher than the rate of 4.83% before the outbreak of the conflict at the end of February.
The rate peaked at close to 6% in April. However, uncertainty remains as the Iran war continues to unfold, in a challenge for Threadneedle Street’s rate-setters.
Official figures due on Wednesday this week are expected to show soaring energy costs drove up UK inflation from 2.6% in June to 2.9% in July, raising City expectations for the central bank to raise borrowing costs. However, separate figures on Tuesday are expected to show a slowdown in the jobs market, which could encourage the Bank to delay taking action.
Financial markets anticipate two quarter-point increases in the Bank’s base rate, from the current level of 3.75%, before the end of next year.
Richard Donnell, an executive director at Zoopla, said: “While the national time to sell has barely moved, that stability is masking a real divide opening up between local markets.”

Max Rocha’s recipes for confit trout salad and grilled courgette with apricot, stracciatella and roasted almonds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:00:15 UTC
14:00:15 KST

Five years after Café Cecilia opened, a handful of dishes have become permanent fixtures, returning to the menu time and again – and this confit trout salad is definitely one of them. During the recent heatwaves, we’ve naturally shifted towards dishes that are best served at room temperature or slightly warm, and both of these recipes reflect that approach. They’re designed to serve two, but can just as easily be scaled up for a larger group. And almost everything can be prepared in advance, making them ideal for entertaining at home.
Confit trout, watercress, pickled cucumber, radish and mustard salad (pictured top)
Prep 10 min
 Cook 45 min
 Serves 2
For the pickles
1 tbsp sugar
  100ml white-wine vinegar
  1 tsp salt 
½ cucumber, finely sliced (on a mandoline, ideally)
5 breakfast radishes,finely sliced (on a mandoline, ideally)
For the trout 
  2 trout fillets (about 150g each), skin on
Salt and pepper 
  300ml sunflower oil
  200ml olive oil 
  3 sprigs thyme
  2 garlic cloves, peeled
For the salad
  6 tbsp good-quality olive oil 
  2 tbsp dijon mustard 
  2 tbsp white-wine vinegar 
  1 bunch watercress (about 80g)
Juice of ½ lemon 
  Extra-virgin olive oil, to finish
4 sprigs chervil, leaves picked
4 sprigs dill, leaves picked
First, make the pickled cucumber by combining 100ml water with the sugar, vinegar and salt in a saucepan, then gradually increase the heat until the sugar dissolves. Pour this over the cucumber and radishes in a bowl, and set aside.
Season the trout, then leave to sit at room temperature for 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, place the sunflower oil, olive oil, thyme and garlic in a pan and heat to 50C (122F) (if you don’t have have a kitchen thermometer, the outside of the pan should feel warm to the touch). Pat the trout dry with kitchen paper, then lay the fish in the warm oil and keep it between 50-55C (120-130F) for 15-20 minutes, until cooked through. Leave to cool a little, then peel off and discard the skin (this is easier to do while the fish is still warm) and leave to cool fully.
Combine the olive oil, mustard and white-wine vinegar. Drain the pickles, then put in a bowl with the watercress and one and a half tablespoons of the vinaigrette (save the rest for other salads in the week). Mix and taste for seasoning, then add a squeeze of lemon juice, a few extra drops of olive oil and a pinch of sea salt and black pepper as required.
Flake each trout fillet into four or five pieces, then divide half of the fish between two plates. Top with half the watercress and pickle salad, lay on the remaining trout, followed by the rest of the pickle mix. Top with the picked herbs, finish with a pinch of sea salt and serve.
Grilled courgette, apricot, stracciatella and roast almonds
Prep 10 min
 Cook 20 min
 Serves 2
1 green courgette
  Extra-virgin olive oil 
1 tsp balsamic vinegar 
Zest of 1 lemon
½ bunch basil, leaves picked 
1 garlic clove, peeled and thinly sliced 
Salt and black pepper
  2 ripe apricots
200g stracciatella
 For the dressing
  45g whole roast almonds
3 tbsp olive oil 
  1 tsp red-wine vinegar 
1 tsp fresh rosemary leaves, chopped
Slice the courgette lengthways into thin strips, brush with olive oil and grill in a hot griddle pan for about two minutes per side, until charred.
Prepare the marinade by putting three tablespoons of olive oil, the balsamic vinegar, lemon zest, basil, garlic and some salt and pepper in a bowl. Fold in the courgettes until evenly coated.
Pound the almonds in a mortar (or roughly chop them), then put in a bowl with the olive oil, vinegar, rosemary and some salt and pepper.
Halve, stone and slice the apricots into thin half-moons. Spoon half the stracciatella on to each plate, followed by the courgettes. Finish with the apricots, dribble a tablespoon of the almond dressing over each portion and serve at once.
- 
  Max Rocha is chef-owner of Café Cecilia, London E8

Rising number of people seeking ADHD diagnosis without treatment, say experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:00:14 UTC
14:00:14 KST

People are increasingly seeking to an obtain an ADHD diagnosis without pursuing treatment, according to experts who have called for more research to understand why.
Some people now regard ADHD as “an identity, rather than a disorder”, with the result that many obtain assessments from poor quality private providers, which lead them to “believe they have a condition needing treatment”, said the psychiatrist Dr Marios Adamou, the founder of the UK Adult ADHD Network.
This has resulted in a growth in complaints against NHS doctors when they are forced to reject low quality assessments, he added.
Adamou had seen recent figures showing that 50% of child patients did not pursue treatment after diagnosis, and observed a similar trend among adult patients in his clinic.
Some patients seek low, non-therapeutic doses of medication instead. “A lot of people would benefit from having amphetamines. You feel better, you can focus better, you can do more. But there hasn’t been a debate that this country should be cognitively augmented to increase productivity with stimulants,” he said.
“Why do people feel they can identify with these conditions? They are manifestations of a societal problem.”
Adamou was speaking ahead of a new Channel 4 documentary airing on 18 August titled The Great ADHD Myth?. It is presented by the NHS psychiatrist Dr Max Pemberton, who concludes that ADHD is a “social construct” rather than a medical condition, and that schools should adapt to better support a wider range of children rather than medicating them into fitting into a restrictive norm.
Adamou said that ADHD was both a social construct and a brain disorder. Brain differences are well established through research, and the diagnostic criteria has undergone “a lot of scientific scrutiny and validation”, he said, but added that in recent years “the ADHD concept has been expanded so much, it’s risking becoming meaningless … it’s socially constructed now, it’s something different than what it actually is.”
He said this phenomenon was fuelled by “challenges with the quality and the regulation of the [ADHD services] market”.
“Most of the assessment in the UK is now provided by the private sector,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any other medical condition where the private sector provides as much care … When you have private providers providing the majority of care in a market system with a diagnosis that is commoditised, and attracts stimulants, you may have issues.”
Despite this, he stressed that there was thought to be underdiagnosis of ADHD. Poor quality diagnoses have created “a double stigma” for many people with the condition. “Not only do you have stigma because you have ADHD, but also there’s stigma about whether you have real ADHD,” he said.
Prof Dinesh Bhugra, the former head of the Royal College of Psychiatrists who features in the documentary, agreed that “there has certainly been a splurge of diagnosis, and we don’t know why that is”.
He said: “The question is why now, and why this? What is it providing? My fear is we medicalise normal human responses because it gives us the power as clinicians and it gives people the label which allows them to either feel they’ve got certain privileges or it gives them certain cachet in society.”
In the documentary, he shares his concerns about the growing role of profiteering private companies supplying services that the NHS is under too much strain to provide. ADHD assessment was “an easy way to make money” for private companies, he said, adding: “Their responsibility is to the shareholders, not the general public.”
Bhugra feared that the UK’s current approach was an American import, where the DSM [Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders]’s checklist-style approach to assessment reflected the demands of insurance companies, and a culture of “health is a commodity and you can buy it and sell it”.
He agreed with the documentary’s message that services should be reformed to take a more holistic approach, bringing together the social, biological and psychological facts of ADHD rather than emphasising medical intervention.
Jessica Lister, a clinical director and consultant nurse at the private provider Care ADHD, feared that the documentary’s message could be harmful. “Dismissing ADHD as a social construct doesn’t just trivialise an established clinical condition – it perpetuates the inequalities faced by people with ADHD across education, health, employment and the justice system,” she said.
“The question here isn’t whether ADHD is a real medical problem – it’s whether systems respond early enough, consistently enough and fairly enough to prevent avoidable harm … The real problems are long waits, inequitable access, inconsistent quality and too little joined-up support across health, education, care and employment.”
Mark Pattison, the chief executive of Care ADHD, said that it was important to differentiate between private providers, adding that his organisation’s clinical governance was as strong as the NHS ADHD and mental health services he had run for 15 years. “Profit should never come before clinical quality. But efficiency isn’t the enemy of it either,” he said.
He added: “Standards need to apply to everyone, not just us. Some NHS trusts have children waiting two, five, even 10 years for an assessment. That’s not safe care, whoever provides it. Some private providers fall short too.”
The Great ADHD Myth? is available to watch and stream on Channel 4 at 8pm, Tuesday 18 August.

Iraq’s ghost villages: Islamic State drove people away – now a new enemy is preventing their return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:00:14 UTC
14:00:14 KST

The first thing that strikes visitors arriving in Faka, a small village in Sinjar district, northern Iraq, is the silence. No children play in the streets. No shops are open. Roofless houses stretch across the hillside, their walls pockmarked by shellfire, while weeds and wild grasses grow through collapsed living rooms.
A decade after Islamic State (IS) swept across the region, war remains visible everywhere. But according to the people who returned, another enemy has quietly taken its place.
“Today, the problem isn’t only IS,” says Rajab Mohammed, 62, the village’s mukhtar, standing above the ruins of Faka. “It’s water. It’s jobs. It’s the future.”
Across Sinjar, abandoned houses now outnumber occupied ones. The battle against IS has ended. The battle to save the villages against drought and neglect has only just begun, and time is not on its side.
Before August 2014, about 150 families lived in Faka. When IS fighters seized the Sinjar region, residents fled as frontlines advanced across north-western Iraq. In August 2014, IS launched what the UN has recognised as a genocide against the ethnic minority Yazidi community. Thousands were killed and more than 6,000 people, mostly women and children, were abducted.
While Faka and the nearby village of Qubq escaped the mass killings that devastated other nearby villages, coalition airstrikes and ground fighting left much of the area destroyed. Today, only about 20 families have returned. The rest have settled elsewhere, discouraged by the lack of reconstruction, jobs and basic services in a region where the climate crisis is making rural livelihoods such as farming increasingly precarious.
“People ask why families don’t come back. The answer is simple. Where would they live? How would they earn a living?” says Aqil Ridha from Qubq.
The UN has ranked the country the fifth most vulnerable to declining water and food availability and extreme heat. Iraqi authorities project that by 2050 the country’s average annual temperature will have risen by 2.5C, with 24 additional days a year crossing extreme heat thresholds. Temperatures in Sinjar this summer have approached 50C.
Rainfall has become increasingly erratic and summers are hotter and longer, while prolonged droughts are reducing agricultural production. The UN’s special representative for Iraq has warned that the country will be able to meet only 15% of its water needs by 2035 if current trends continue.
In rural areas, where farming remains the principal source of income, the issues of climate and migration have become inseparable. The International Organization for Migration has recorded more than 186,000 people displaced by climate-related factors across Iraq as of September 2025.
In the village of Tal Jado’o, Bahjat Othman Hasan walks between ruined homes that have never been rebuilt. The roads remain little more than dirt tracks. Electricity is intermittent. Before the war, more than 200 people lived here. Today, barely 50 remain. “People didn’t leave because they wanted to,” he says. “They left because they couldn’t live here any more.”
Parts of the surrounding countryside are still contaminated by unexploded ordnance left behind after IS was driven out. But the greatest concern now lies beneath the surface, where groundwater levels continue to fall every year. “Years ago, you could reach water at around 10 metres,” says Hasan. “Today, we must drill to around 25 metres. Every year it becomes more expensive.”
Not far from Tal Jado’o, the village of Al-Sajea shows what happens once that tipping point is passed. Before the war, 37 families lived here. Today all 24 houses still standing are severely damaged, their rooms and courtyards overrun by hurfeish, the spiny, purple-flowered wild milk thistle that has colonised abandoned fields and ruins across the region. Nobody lives here any more.
“Everybody went to Tal Afar [a city in northern Iraq],” says Asef Hasan Ali, 43, one of the few people who still comes back at all. He lives in Tal Afar, but during the agricultural season he stays in a caravan parked at the edge of the village, close to the fields he still works. “For families, it’s impossible: everything was bombed, nobody can live here.”
Only days before our visit, 19-year-old Smain from the village of Qazal Quyu says his family’s vegetable garden burned to the ground after a dust devil whipped across neighbouring fields, triggering an electrical spark that ignited dry vegetation. These rapidly rotating columns of hot air, common during Iraq’s increasingly intense summers, have become another symbol of a changing climate.
The villages are not simply losing people, they are losing a generation. Village schools have fewer pupils every year. Those who complete secondary education rarely return after university. Others head directly into construction jobs in the cities of Mosul or Erbil, where wages, although modest, are more reliable than farming.
“Almost all my friends want to leave. Sometimes I want to leave, too. But if I go, who will help my parents?” says Smain.
